news.title: Arnold Schwarzenegger celebrates his 79th birthday showing off his iron-pumping workout, fit physique
news.text:
Arnold Schwarzenegger flaunted his legendary muscles while marking his 79th birthday.

The “Terminator” star was pictured pumping iron in what appeared to be Los Angeles in a pair of celebratory birthday pics Thursday. 

In both snapshots, he wore a black t-shirt and matching shorts, and accessorized with a gold watch and a pair of sunglasses as he displayed his massive arms for his followers.

In the caption, the “Predator” star plugged his Pump Club — a fitness community app that offers customized nutrition tracking, workout routines, and more.

“I turn 79 today. I don’t want any gifts,” he wrote in part. “Instead, my team and I are turning the fitness industry upside down.” 

Fans of the former governor of California flocked to the comments thread to gush over his ripped physique, even as he approaches 80. 

“Happy birthday, 50 years ago you were training with one of the best physiques ever and 50 years later today you are still training with one of the best physiques ever for your age!” one person remarked, while another enthused, “HBD legend!🔥” 

A third chimed in, “Health, happiness and best of life to you 🎂 You’ve inspired an entire generation and still continue to,” while a fourth wrote, “thanks for inspiring me all those years ago to follow my dream! ✨🙏” 

Schwarzenegger — whose 28-year-old son, Joseph Baena, is following in his famous dad’s footsteps with a bodybuilding career — again defied age last month, when he stepped out with much-younger girlfriend Heather Milligan.

In a rare public appearance, the couple — who began dating 14 years ago — were spotted at the Austrian World Summit in Vienna, Austria, in June.

In a photo from the event, Milligan, 51, and the “True Lies” actor were joined by former US Vice President Kamala Harris and President Alexander Van der Bellen of Austria.

The “Kindergarten Cop” actor’s fitness-themed birthday upload comes on the heels of decades of fitness accomplishments. 

In a 2023 interview, the seven-time Mr. Olympia winner admitted to struggling with body image as he ages — even despite being more fit than the “majority” of people his age.

“I kind of smile because every day I do look in a mirror and I say, ‘Yep, you suck,’” he told Howard Stern at the time. 

“When you’ve been hailed for years as this supreme body, and you have the definition and you see the veins coming down your abs, and you see veins on top of your chest and then … you roll the clock 50 years and you’re standing there and you don’t see that anymore,” he lamented. 

He added, “I never, ever thought about that when I was 30 years old or 40 years old that this [was] going to happen. It just sucks.”
news.summary: Schwarzenegger is a seven-time Mr. Olympia winner.

news.title: Charli xcx hosts fan Q&A at Chicago’s Reckless Records
news.text:
Even with Lollapalooza in full swing at Grant Park, some fans of British pop star Charli xcx found themselves inWicker Park yesterday for a conversation with fans ahead of the musician’s headlining Lollapalooza performance Friday.

Tickets to the sold-out event were an approachable $30 and included a copy of the artist’s new album.

While an ice cream truck-turned-merch-stand blared tracks off her new album “Music, Fashion, Film,” fans sang, sweated and met new friends as they stood in line outside of the Reckless Records on Milwaukee Avenue.

The first two groups of fans in line had traveled from Alabama, Miami, and New York for Lollapalooza. After hours of standing next to each other, they realized they knew mutual people on socials and said this meetup might lead to future hangouts.

Two 17-year-olds sitting on the sidewalk under a blue umbrella had been in line since 11:30 a.m. for the 3:30 p.m. event. “I’ve never seen Charli live, so this is my opportunity,” said Addison Davis. “She’s just going to do a Q&A, but it’s the closest thing I’m getting.” Davis couldn’t get tickets to Lollapalooza but said this was a moment to make the most of it.

Charli xcx’s new album, “Music, Fashion, Film,” is a departure from her sixth studio album, “Brat,” which topped charts with its synthy club tracks and became a social media phenomenon, even making an appearance in former Vice President Kamala Harris’ campaign.

The first track released from the new album, called “Rock Music,” sparked chatter online because of its heavy guitar riffs, prompting fans to wonder if the musician was moving away from danceable electronic music. But John Norat from Miami, Florida, who was standing in line for the event, had a response to some of the backlash

“There was a whole discourse about ‘the dancefloor is dead’ thing, but I think the music she’s making now is still from the dance world, but it’s rock,” Norat opined. “The most important thing about this era is the live performances and the cadence, how she carries herself on stage. She’s a rock star, and I’m just so excited.”

Victoria Adler, who was also waiting to see the pop star in person on Thursday, said she believes this album showcases Charli xcx’s deep knowledge of music. She went to two free “Music, Fashion, Film” screenings of a related film and is loving how fan focused it all feels.

“All these secret shows she’s doing that are pop-ups, it’s just refreshing in this time to see an artist as big as she is post-‘Brat’ really giving it back to the fans.”

The sold-out event inside the record shop was closed to media, and press photography was not allowed inside. Fans who had wrist bracelets and were allowed in crowded the musician, who spent nearly 40 minutes taking questions, graciously answering everything from what kind of lip gloss was in her purse to her thoughts about public transit.

She talked about how she made the album for herself, not the fans. She added that positive reception is a bonus, not the driving force behind her creativity.

Charli xcx headlines Lollapalooza Friday in one of the most female-forward lineups in the festival’s history. Fellow women headliners include Olivia Dean and Blackpink’s Jennie on Saturday and Canadian pop queen Tate McRae, J-pop star Ado and the xx’s Romy Madley Croft on Sunday.
news.author: Lynnea Domienik

news.title: Trump's 'twitches and glitches' alarm expert amid fresh health concerns
news.text:
Speech-language pathologist Hillary Shea is seeing a number of red flags indicating President Donald Trump's cognitive decline is getting worse.

She elaborated on what she could see, in her expertise as a clinician, on the David Pakman Show on Thursday.

"We've observed in Donald Trump what appears to be a diminished range of vocabulary, that the sort of number of words he uses has diminished over time," said Pakman. "We've seen these, what I call glitches, where when he gets a word wrong, there's a physical thing where a shoulder goes up, and he seems to almost reboot, for lack of a better term ... am I making something out of nothing, or are there clinically relevant observations that we can make here?"

Shea confirmed these are all, in fact, trouble signs.

"What's happening within the brain networks is that the brain is supposed to be regulating and suppressing unwanted motor movements," she said, noting that this isn't well developed in kids, and also deteriorates as people age. "The frontal lobe should be suppressing unwanted motor movements like those twitches."

Pakman then noted a study during the 2024 presidential campaign finding that former President Joe Biden's vocabulary only diminished slightly from years ago, and former Vice President Kamala Harris' didn't at all — but Trump's diminished significantly. "Is that clinically relevant in some way?"

"It's absolutely clinically relevant," said Shea. "That signifies that the brain deterioration in Trump is much more significant than in Biden ... his vocabulary is very repetitive. It's very monosyllabic, which sometimes is going to have to do with the fact that it's really hard for Trump to say multisyllabic words right now." His "perseveration" on topics like the 2020 election is worrisome as well, she said.

The topic then turned to the Montreal Cognitive Assessment, the dementia test Trump constantly brags about "acing" — which Shea clarified isn't really a good sign.

"If he actually got a perfect score, a 30 out of 30, it honestly tells me nothing ... even people who have dementia, who come into my office who already have a diagnosis, can still sometimes get 30 out of 30 on that test," said Shea. "So 30 out of 30 doesn't actually tell me much. The fact that he has taken it multiple times over the course of a year and a half tells me way more." What that means, she said, is "they're looking for something, whether it's decline or medication, how is he responding to medication?"

Pakman later noted that he has seen a deterioration of Trump's motor skills as well, including his inability to cap a Sharpie and fumbling with Tic Tacs at Lindsey Graham's funeral — something Shea isn't as thorough of an expert in, but which she agreed was troubling.

"The brain controls everything," said Shea. "So, fine motor control of your articulators is the same thing as fine motor control with your fingers." She noted that his handwriting has shown signs of deterioration as well. "It's not just the muscles themselves. It's the proprioception, where his body is in space and what his arms and legs and things are doing. It's visual perceptual processing. It involves more than we think. So when you have general brain decline ... everything becomes affected."

news.title: NY Rep. Mike Lawler’s race now a ‘toss-up’ as Dems target battleground district that could flip Congress
news.text:
US Rep. Mike Lawler’s re-election race vs. Democrat Cait Conley is now a “toss-up,” according to an independent analyst’s assessment released Thursday.

The Center for Politics at the University of Virginia initially rated the race for New York’s battleground 17th Congressional District as “lean Republican” based on Lawler’s “impressive victories” in 2022 and 2024 despite the district voting Democratic for president.

But the race for the Hudson Valley seat in one of the few Empire State swing districts has turned the race into the most closely watched in the state as it’s considered key to which party ends up controlling Congress in 2027. 

“Lawler, who holds a district based in Westchester and Rockland counties, drew what appeared to be his strongest potential challenger, [Army] veteran Cait Conley (D), in last month’s primary, and Conley also got the ballot line for the Working Families Party,” the analysis by the center’s “Sabato’s Crystal Ball” said.

“The lack of a divided field may aid Conley in NY-17,” Sabato Crystal Ball’s managing editor Kyle Kondik said.

Overall, the analysis released Thursday moved five House races from lean Republican to toss-up, including Lawler’s seat. The other races are in Florida, North Carolina and Pennsylvania.

Partisans on both sides have conducted surveys showing their candidate ahead, but only narrowly.

A poll conducted by GOP-leaning co/efficient showed Lawler with 50% of the vote to Cait Conley’s 45%, just a five-point spread.

A survey conducted by the political action committee for House Democrats had Conley leading Lawler 51% to 45%.

The Cook Political Report also recently rated the swing district contest a toss-up, while the Fox News Power Rankings moved the race from even to “Lean D.”

Lawler first took the seat in 2022 when he defeated former Rep. Sean Patrick Maloney, then the chairman of the House Democratic Campaign Committee.

He handily won re-election in 2024, beating former lefty Rep. Mondaire Jones by six points despite the district going blue for Kamala Harris in the presidential election.

Conley, an Army veteran, won a five-way primary to win the Democratic nomination — a more mainstream or moderate challenger better suited to make a run in the suburban district that includes all or parts of Westchester, Putnam and Dutchess counties.

Lawler, a former state Assembly member, has fought to largely restore the state and local tax deduction on federal income tax returns and has been a staunch supporter of Israel.

Conley, a West Point Military Academy graduate, worked as director of counterterrorism on the National Security Council in the Biden administration. She previously served in the US Army and was deployed overseas six times.

Conley campaign spokeswoman Maddy Rosen said Conley would “fight to rein in Washington corruption” and usher in a “better, more affordable future for working families. 

“Hudson Valley voters are clearly sick and tired of being thrown under the bus by party-first politician Mike Lawler, who votes with Donald Trump 100% of the time, and are eager for a leader like Cait Conley, whose entire career has been in service to the American people,” Rosen said.

“And unlike Mike, who spends his time cozying up to the corporations and special interests funding his campaign, Cait isn’t taking a single vote for granted.”

Lawler’s campaign manager Ciro Riccardi shrugged off the new analysis.

“Democrats threw everything at Mike Lawler in 2022 and 2024 and lost both times. Nothing has changed,” Riccardi said. “He leads Cait Conley by 5 in an independent survey, winning independents by 15 points, and has five times her cash in the bank. If [House Democratic Minority Leader] Hakeem Jeffries wants to set another fortune on fire in the Hudson Valley, be our guest. We’ll bring the marshmallows.”

Overall, the assessment gives Democrats a slight advantage to win back the House, though not as strongly as they did in President Trump’s first term in 2018, because of GOP-led redrawing of congressional districts in some states.

“Democrats remain favored to flip the House majority in November, but Republicans have a path, too,” Sabato’s Crystal Ball said.

“Republicans have 208 seats at least leaning to them, Democrats have 207, and there are now 20 Toss-ups. This gives both parties pathways to a majority, but we’d still expect Democrats to do better among the Toss-ups. Our best guess at this point would be Democrats winning a majority in the low-to-mid 220s.”

The Center for Politics at UVA was founded by professor Larry Sabato, its director, and the “Crystal Ball” analysis was started by and is named after him.
news.summary: An independent analyst rates the race between 2-term incumbent Republican Rep. Mike Lawler and Democrat Cait Conley in the Hudson Valley's swing 17th House District as a toss-up.
news.author: Carl Campanile

news.title: Fixing Homelessness Means Killing the Homeless Industrial Complex
news.text:
In 2020, according to the HDIS data, there were 249,000 homeless people in California. These are people who received some form of state-funded homeless services. By 2025, just five years later, the number of homeless people in the state jumped to 358,784, an increase of 109,784 people on state benefits. Percentage-wise, that’s off the charts at 44%. A 44% increase in five years.

In 2020, California taxpayers funded homeless programs to the tune of $1.2 billion. By 2025, that number jumped to $1.5 billion. This money was spent on a range of social services, including the Homeless Housing, Assistance, and Prevention (HHAP) program.

Doesn’t seem like there is much prevention going on.

It’s difficult to compare California’s data to other states, because each state has its own way of counting the homeless and tracking the usage of social services for the homeless. Still, in the state of New York, core state funding dedicated to the homeless totaled $2.5 billion to $3 billion in 2025. This includes shelter and service costs, but again, the state makes it difficult to determine precisely where all that money is going.

Texas has better data any way that you look at it. The numbers are better, and the transparency of the data is better. That state has just over 51,000 people who accessed homeless services in 2025. In terms of funding, Texas allocates a small fraction of what California and New York put out, not only in terms of total spending, but also in per-capita spending when you overlay this data against the number of homeless people. The Texas state budget is roughly $15-$25 million per year.

What this means is Texas spends roughly $490 per year on each homeless person who accesses services in that state. California spends about $4,180 per year on each homeless person who accesses state services. New York’s data is too fuzzy to make an apples-to-apples comparison here, and that’s an issue. Or, maybe a better way to say it is, that’s a symptom of a larger problem.

The amount of money flying around in the name of combatting homelessness is mind-boggling, often impossible to track, almost always spent with no accountability, and there is no real way to measure its effectiveness in actually solving the homelessness problem. Along the way, though, everyone gets a cut.

Kevin Dahlgren, a homeless advocate and activist, takes a boots-on-the-ground approach to trying to help the homeless. He has dubbed the problem here the “homeless industrial complex.”

The term conjures up memories of a massive problem President Dwight D. Eisenhower once identified in the “military-industrial complex.” When Eisenhower coined his term, he was talking about how certain forces within government and outside of government will constantly pursue war so as to feed the companies and industries that prosper from war, not peace.

Dahlgren’s homeless industrial complex makes a similar statement. There are too many people, nonprofits, NGOs, state agencies, and others who make far too much money in the name of combatting homelessness to expect that any of them would want to see an end to the problem. The goal of a homeless industrial complex is to grow and perpetuate the problem.

Dahlgren says he wants to end homelessness by empowering, not enabling, those on the streets.

“I have encountered the same homeless people during outreach visits, encampment sweeps, overdose reversals, hospital discharges, shelter referrals, nonprofit events, and police responses. Every agency involved can document that it did something. Someone made contact, completed an assessment, offered a referral, handed out a brochure, or entered the person’s name into a database. Then I return days, weeks, or months later, and the person is still on the same sidewalk. That is one of the biggest failures of the homelessness system: It rewards activity, not results,” Dahlgren wrote on his Substack blog recently.

When it comes to the biggest and most well-funded systems, it’s no accident that the homelessness program is growing, not improving. These systems tend to be in blue states and are overseen by Democrat administrations. That’s no accident, either.

Common sense indicates that these systems aren’t faulty. They are working as designed, which is to allow for the growth of the homeless, and even to incentivize it through certain state programs. The systems are often designed to make tracking spending and accountability nearly impossible, which opens the door to fraud, waste, and corruption.

In June 2026, the federal HUD program suspended funding to the Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority (LAHSA) after identifying a broad range of serious problems that included LAHSA’s “false statements and its irresponsible actions and failures, including its lack of financial management, internal controls, and safeguards against conflicts of interest, which pose a threat to the public, HUD’s mission, and the stewardship of taxpayer dollars.”

Among the many serious issues identified, HUD reported, “In August 2023, LAHSA could not even determine whether it used funding to pay for empty hotel rooms, because it failed to record when individuals exited transitional motel housing.”

In 2025, LAHSA couldn’t even provide documentation to verify the very existence of 2,300 housing sites for which it was responsible.

In January of this year, the Los Angeles Times reported that one local man was arrested on charges of wire fraud on allegations that he fleeced the city’s homeless services bureaucracy for $23 million. The charges allege that he misappropriated funds from his Hyde Park-based program Abundant Blessings.

In March 2025, the Times reported that “an audit by the global consulting firm Alvarez & Marsal found that the city was unable to track exactly how much it spent on homeless programs and did not rigorously reconcile spending with services provided, making it impossible to judge how well the services worked or whether they were even provided.”

In California, fraud, corruption, and waste strictly in the homeless industrial complex are so pervasive that it could be its own full-time beat and keep a team of reporters very busy. 

On matters like this, they say, “follow the money.” That's a good rule of thumb here. But the people who designed these systems did so precisely so you can't easily follow the money. These same people are working just as hard to keep that money flowing, and to do that, job number one is to make sure there is an endless supply of homeless to “serve.”

news.title: Is This a Red Flag for the GOP in This Year's Midterms?
news.text:
But that’s no reason to get complacent, and there are red flags that suggest the GOP shouldn’t assume all is going to end well.

Let's be honest here: nothing about November is decided yet, and that cuts both ways. I still believe Republicans have real advantages heading into the midterms, and I am not walking that back. But confidence is not the same thing as complacency, and there are warning signs. If Democrats manage to pull off a win despite what’s working against them, President Donald Trump's legislative agenda grinds to a halt for the rest of his term.

The clearest warning sign comes from CNN's Harry Enten, who has been tracking the shift for months. Enten told CNN anchor Kate Bolduan this week that voters under 50 have turned sharply against Trump, and the numbers he laid out are startling. "We are talking about an absolutely huge shift, a 180," Enten said. "Young voters are fed up and they're taking their anger out on President Trump."

According to Enten, Kamala Harris led Trump among voters under 50 by just three points back in the fall of 2024. Trump's net approval among that same group has since collapsed to minus 41 points, a swing Enten called "a shift of 38 points away from the president of the United States." Voters 50 and older have moved against Trump too, but by less than half as much.

ICYMI: Things Got a Bit Nasty Between John Fetterman and Bernie Sanders

That shift isn't staying confined to Trump's approval rating, either. Enten's polling shows Democrats now leading Republicans in the generic House ballot among younger voters by 17 points, up from just four points in the fall of 2024. Voters 50 and older, by contrast, have barely moved. "If you're a Republican in Congress and you think you're going to escape the unpopularity that President Trump has amongst younger voters, you got another thing coming," Enten warned. He went further, calling it "a Titanic-type of shift away from the Republican Party and to the Democratic Party," and noted that among the most motivated younger voters, Democrats now hold a stunning 46-point advantage in the House ballot, up from just two points in 2024. "These are the types of numbers that blue waves are made of," he said.

Now, that sounds bad, but it’s not the worst thing. See, here's the problem with taking that data at face value. Younger voters are consistently the least reliable segment of the electorate in midterm elections. They already turn out at lower rates than older voters in every cycle, but the drop-off between presidential and midterm turnout is far steeper among the young than among any other age group. Enten is measuring a real shift in sentiment, but sentiment isn't turnout. The voters angriest at Trump right now are also the voters most likely to stay home in November, and that gap could blunt whatever wave Democrats are hoping to ride.

None of that means Republicans can afford to sit back and assume the numbers will sort themselves out. Enten is documenting something real, and dismissing it outright would be its own form of complacency. The GOP's path to holding its majorities still runs through turning out the voters most inclined to show up, while hoping the voters most inclined to punish Trump keep doing what young voters usually do in midterms: staying home.
news.author: Matt Margolis

news.title: ABC Sounds Alarm On FCC License Review, Says Trump Is Retaliating For Coverage
news.text:
One of the nation’s largest broadcasters is accusing the Trump administration of retaliation, alleging the Federal Communications Commission is unfairly policing ABC and ABC-owned stations by conducting an unprecedented early review of its broadcast licenses because the president personally dislikes its programming.

“The retaliation against ABC is a signal to every media company in the country: accommodate the Administration’s view of what news coverage should look like or pay the price,” lawyers for the network said in a Wednesday filing. 

Disney-owned ABC has found itself a target of the administration’s attacks on the press as President Donald Trump tests his power to weaponize government agencies in an effort to intimidate and deter the media from covering him in a negative light. 

During his second term, the president has repeatedly demanded the network have its licenses revoked and called for the firing of late-night host Jimmy Kimmel over political remarks he made. The FCC announced the early review of ABC’s broadcast licenses earlier this year, along with a number of other investigations into the network. 

Most recently, the president demanded ABC — and any other network that refused to air his July 16 primetime speech — have its licenses revoked. 

Now, the company is warning that the administration is making a clear attack on the First Amendment and threatening all broadcasters’ freedoms, claiming the express purpose of the FCC’s actions is “to punish ABC for the content of its speech and to chill future speech that the Administration dislikes.”

“Even if any violation were ever substantiated, the [FCC] has a graduated set of well established remedies far short of the corporate death penalty of license non-renewal,” the company’s lawyers argued. “That the agency reached first for the most extreme sanction in its arsenal, before making any finding at all, reveals its true objective: to chill not only ABC, but every broadcaster watching.”

The FCC made its unprecedented move in April when it announced it would require ABC to file early broadcast license renewal applications for all eight of its television stations, just one day after Trump publicly chastised Kimmel for a joke he made about first lady Melania Trump. 

Before that, the commission had not called for renewal applications ahead of schedule for more than 50 years and never once demanded simultaneous applications from a group of stations.

“The Commission’s departure from those norms lays bare what is really going on: the Administration is retaliating against ABC for the exercise of its First Amendment rights,” the filing reads.

Despite Trump’s best efforts, the FCC would still face significant obstacles if it ever attempted to strip ABC of its licenses, as it would need to prove that the network had abused rules and engaged in misconduct.

Trump’s attacks on ABC began while he was still running for a second term, when he accused the network’s moderators of unfairly fact-checking him during a 2024 debate with then-Vice President Kamala Harris, asserting the FCC “ought to take away their license.”

Shortly after returning to the White House, Trump’s newly appointed FCC Chair Brendan Carr asked the agency’s Enforcement Bureau to open an investigation into the network for potentially violating equal employment opportunity regulations by promoting DEI efforts in the workplace. 

In September, after Kimmel made an on-air joke about Charlie Kirk’s alleged killer, Carr issued an ultimatum to the network: “We can do this the easy way or the hard way. These companies can find ways to take action on Kimmel, or there is going to be additional work for the FCC ahead.”

ABC suspended Kimmel’s show for roughly a week before reinstalling the program after facing backlash from the public and political leaders on both sides of the aisle, including Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), who called Carr’s threats “dangerous as hell.”

But the FCC continued its pursuit of ABC in February when it launched an investigation into “The View,” alleging a violation of an equal opportunities rule by hosting Democratic Texas Senate candidate James Talarico. 

Lawyers for ABC noted that the “View” investigation was launched just a month after the FCC reversed decades of precedent that exempted late-night and daytime talk shows from the equal opportunity requirements.
news.author: Caroline Wilburn

During his second term, the president has repeatedly demanded the network have its licenses revoked and called for the firing of late-night host Jimmy Kimmel over political remarks he made. The FCC announced the early review of ABC’s broadcast licenses earlier this year, along with a number of other investigations into the network. 

Most recently, the president demanded ABC — and any other network that refused to air his July 16 primetime speech — have its licenses revoked. 

Now, the company is warning that the administration is making a clear attack on the First Amendment and threatening all broadcasters’ freedoms, claiming the express purpose of the FCC’s actions is “to punish ABC for the content of its speech and to chill future speech that the Administration dislikes.”

“Even if any violation were ever substantiated, the [FCC] has a graduated set of well established remedies far short of the corporate death penalty of license non-renewal,” the company’s lawyers argued. “That the agency reached first for the most extreme sanction in its arsenal, before making any finding at all, reveals its true objective: to chill not only ABC, but every broadcaster watching.”

The FCC made its unprecedented move in April when it announced it would require ABC to file early broadcast license renewal applications for all eight of its television stations, just one day after Trump publicly chastised Kimmel for a joke he made about first lady Melania Trump. 

Before that, the commission had not called for renewal applications ahead of schedule for more than 50 years and never once demanded simultaneous applications from a group of stations.

“The Commission’s departure from those norms lays bare what is really going on: the Administration is retaliating against ABC for the exercise of its First Amendment rights,” the filing reads.

Despite Trump’s best efforts, the FCC would still face significant obstacles if it ever attempted to strip ABC of its licenses, as it would need to prove that the network had abused rules and engaged in misconduct.

Trump’s attacks on ABC began while he was still running for a second term, when he accused the network’s moderators of unfairly fact-checking him during a 2024 debate with then-Vice President Kamala Harris, asserting the FCC “ought to take away their license.”

Shortly after returning to the White House, Trump’s newly appointed FCC Chair Brendan Carr asked the agency’s Enforcement Bureau to open an investigation into the network for potentially violating equal employment opportunity regulations by promoting DEI efforts in the workplace. 

In September, after Kimmel made an on-air joke about Charlie Kirk’s alleged killer, Carr issued an ultimatum to the network: “We can do this the easy way or the hard way. These companies can find ways to take action on Kimmel, or there is going to be additional work for the FCC ahead.”

ABC suspended Kimmel’s show for roughly a week before reinstalling the program after facing backlash from the public and political leaders on both sides of the aisle, including Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), who called Carr’s threats “dangerous as hell.”

But the FCC continued its pursuit of ABC in February when it launched an investigation into “The View,” alleging a violation of an equal opportunities rule by hosting Democratic Texas Senate candidate James Talarico. 

Lawyers for ABC noted that the “View” investigation was launched just a month after the FCC reversed decades of precedent that exempted late-night and daytime talk shows from the equal opportunity requirements.

news.title: It's Official: Shame Has Died in Politics, and the Media Killed It
news.text:
Politico clearly wants the data from its latest survey to build a narrative about MAGA voters. The subtext, however, lands more fully on consistent polling about the Protection Racket Media. 

Politico's survey with Public First focuses on scandal tolerance in both parties, and needless to say, the data has plenty of applications in this cycle. Politico concludes that Donald Trump's voter base will forgive just about any kind of misconduct. However, the phrasing of the question matters, especially one word in particular:

The POLITICO Poll finds President Donald Trump’s MAGA supporters are the most loyal of any group of voters — with majorities saying they would stick by GOP candidates confronted with an array of scandals, from a DUI conviction or accepting lobbyist gifts to more serious accusations including domestic violence, sexual assault and antisemitic social media posts.Two-thirds of self-identified MAGA Trump voters say they would continue supporting a GOP candidate accused of sexual assault — 13 percentage points higher than the share of Trump 2024 voters writ large, which include those who do not identify as MAGA. By comparison, 40 percent of voters who backed former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024 would continue backing a Democratic candidate accused of sexual assault.Seventy-two percent of MAGA Trump voters say they would stick with a GOP candidate accused of domestic violence, more than 10 percentage points higher than the overall share of Trump 2024 voters who would back a GOP candidate (61 percent). Thirty-nine percent of Harris voters say they’d stick with a Democrat accused of domestic violence.

Note well the word "accused" in these questions. They are not asking about proven scandals, but mere allegations of scandals. It doesn't take a genius to figure out why that distinction matters to MAGA voters, or Republicans more generally. In just one instance alone, as my pal Mark Judge has related extensively here at Hot Air, Democrats and the media inflated an ambiguous allegation about Justice Brett Kavanaugh's teen years into an entire scandal industry, with absolutely no corroboration whatsoever. Even the witnesses cited by Christine Blasey Ford refused to back up her claims about a party that Ford could neither date nor locate, and one of them accused Ford and her allies of attempting to pressure her into corroboration. Nevertheless, those allegations continue to follow Kavanaugh, thanks in large part to the media that declared open season on Kavanaugh during and after his confirmation. 

That pattern goes back decades. Democrats still hail Anita Hill for her unsubstantiated claims against Justice Clarence Thomas in 1991, even though women who worked for him testified to his character and proper behavior in the office – and not a hint of harassing behavior has emerged since. The media and Democrats have spent the last decade making all sorts of scandal allegations against Donald Trump, again mainly without substantiation. That was their entire 2024 electoral strategy, and the election showed just how tired voters have become with it. They're teeing up the scandal train in Texas against Ken Paxton too, but the survey shows how uninterested voters have become with scandalmongering targeting Republicans and conservatives. 

No one's listening to accusations and allegations any longer. The media still has not learned about the fable of the boy who cried "wolf," clearly. Voters don't factor allegations into their calculations because they no longer trust the elite media that attempts to sell these as legitimate scandals. There is a reason why Gallup's surveys show newspapers and TV news rank lowest in confidence among all American institutions except Congress. 

What's more, Politico demonstrates why people don't trust the media in its framing of the responses. They attempt to claim that Kamala Harris voters have higher standards:

Harris 2024 voters, however, drew a line. Facing some scandals, such as a Democratic candidate accepting gifts from lobbyists or accused of domestic violence or sexual assault, more Harris voters would either stay home or vote Republican than stick with their party’s nominee.That dynamic has played out on the campaign trail. In Maine, Platner weathered months of controversy, including over past Reddit posts and a tattoo that resembled a Nazi symbol, and only dropped out of the race after POLITICO’s report that a woman said he forced her to have sex with him, an allegation he denies.

This is drizzly effluvium, to put it mildly. The tattoo didn't just resemble a Nazi symbol – it was specifically the Nazi SS Totenkopf, which Platner lied about when he began running for the Senate nomination. Leading Democrats and progressives stuck with Platner anyway, even after Lyndsey Fifield came forward to allege domestic violence. Platner won the primary anyway with 70% of the vote, while Ro Khanna argued that voters should send Platner to the Senate anyway as a measure of "grace and redemption." Bernie Sanders, Liz Warren, and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez all maintained their endorsements. The New York Times attempted to "tamp and tame" Lyndsey's allegation by framing her as a Republican operative.

The only reason why Platner's political support dissipated was that a Democrat stepped up to reveal his sexual assault on her. Jenny Racicot got disgusted by the way the NY Times and Democrats treated Lyndsey and finally put an end to Der Oysterführer, but that wasn't because of any principled stand by "Kamala Harris voters." It's because the GOP was ready to go full tilt on Platner in Maine and make him a poster boy in every other midterm campaign. 

Nearly every Protection Racket Media outlet covered the Platner scandal series as another "Republicans pounce™" story, until Platner finally had to withdraw. And Politico wonders why Republicans put almost no trust in 'allegations' and 'accusations' in the media? Come on, man.

Unfortunately, the result of all this biased scandalmongering has been to render shame an ineffective disincentive in politics. That's not a new development; Platner wouldn't have run in the first place if shame hadn't already been killed in politics. It didn't start with Trump either. It started – or at least metastasized – when Democrats and the media that hyperventilated over Hill's unsubstantiated allegations of sexual harassment suddenly decided a few years later that perjury related to sexual harassment and the exploiting of an intern was just a private issue when a Democrat did it. Shame died in the 1990s, both in politics and in media bias.

news.title: Kamala Harris’ new $8M mansion is in a neighborhood with virtually no black residents
news.text:
Despite a career-long commitment to combating racial disparities in housing and touting the importance of living among Black people, former Vice President Kamala Harris’ new California mansion is situated in a neighborhood with virtually no racial diversity.

Harris’ new 4,000-square-foot property, which reports indicate she acquired for $8.15 million, is located in the exclusive seaside community of Point Dume and includes ocean views, multiple wine fridges, private golf greens and enough parking to accommodate five vehicles.

Point Dume is situated entirely within Census tract 8004.08, which the Census Bureau’s American Community Survey estimated was just 0.2% Black and roughly 94% White as of 2019.

Harris’ choice of neighborhood may surprise longtime observers given past comments she has made about the importance of living among other Black Americans.

“When you’re at (a historically Black college or university), and especially one with the size and with the history of Howard University — and also in the context of also being in D.C., which was known forever as being ‘Chocolate City’ — it just becomes about you understanding that there is a whole world of people who are like you,” Harris told a Washington Post reporter in 2019, reflecting on her experience growing up in primarily White social circles then attending a historically Black college in a predominantly African American city.

“It was more, for me, about the numerosity than it was the diversity, I grew up in a community where there were many representations of diversity,” she added. “Going to Howard, there were so many (Black people)! And they’re all in your age group, in your phase of life.”

Now, however, Harris has chosen to put roots down in a community that at least one group has accused of trying to keep their beaches closed off to minorities.

“Despite the veneer of a laid back community of surfers who are one with nature, there are barriers to access that keep most BIPOC people away,” a pair of non-White surfers wrote in a 2025 review of Harris’s new neighborhood.

Harris spent a sizable portion of her career working to tear down similar barriers.

In 2012, as California’s attorney general, for instance, she joined a Supreme Court brief arguing that the Fair Housing Act can be enforced when policies have a “disparate impact” across different racial groups, even if the policies themselves are racially neutral.

As a presidential candidate, she proposed $100 billion in assistance for families in historically redlined communities and as vice president she promoted the Biden administration’s efforts to combat racial bias in home appraisals.

During Harris’ 2020 presidential campaign, she faced questions about the authenticity of her African American identity due to her Indian and Jamaican heritage and upbringing in affluent, primarily White areas. The attacks resurfaced in 2024, when then-candidate Donald Trump accused Harris of using her Black identity for political gain.

Harris caught flak during the 2024 campaign for identifying with Oakland, California, even though she spent most of her childhood growing up in Berkeley, California, which was significantly less racially diverse. As a teenager, she moved to Montreal, another predominantly White city, with her mother.

Doug Emhoff, Harris’ husband, is also White.

Harris has returned to the headlines in recent weeks amid speculation that she may make a third run for the presidency in 2028.

A representative for the former vice president did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital Wednesday.

news.title: Elon Musk Is Firing Up the Vote-Buying Machine Again
news.text:
Elon Musk has sent conflicting messages over the past year about politics, at one point getting so frustrated with Donald Trump that he pledged to start his own political party. That idea went nowhere fast, and he claimed he would back off from any political spending in the future. But that was a lie.

The SpaceX CEO is ready to really throw his weight around for the midterm elections in November. Musk has authorized his super PAC to spend as much as $120 million helping Republicans, according to a new report from the New York Times. In May, it was reported Musk had already spent $85 million on this cycle, making him the third-largest donor for the midterms to that point.

Musk’s PAC, known as America PAC, will focus on the so-called ground game, knocking on doors and helping drive voter turnout, according to the Times and previous reporting by Axios. America PAC will be coordinating with other Republican groups and will first target U.S. Senate races in five states: Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Michigan, and Ohio.

Discussions about also helping knock doors for the Senate races in North Carolina, Georgia, and Texas are ongoing, according to the Times. And there will also be a presence for U.S. House races in California, Wisconsin, and Washington, among others. Chris Young, considered to be Musk’s top political advisor, will lead the efforts. Young worked on Musk’s DOGE, the so-called Department of Government Efficiency.

Musk spent nearly $300 million to help elect Republicans like President Trump during the 2024 elections, which bought him the opportunity to establish DOGE. Musk and his young goons (remember Big Balls?) took a chainsaw to the federal government, unlawfully dissolving USAID and helping cut the federal workforce by about 300,000 people.

The damage to foreign aid and public health was incalculable, though some people have put some numbers to the estimated death toll. At least 750,000 people have died, though Musk denies that fact in the face of overwhelming evidence.

Musk’s PAC fueled door-knocking initiatives in swing states during the 2024 election, helping Trump secure a victory over Kamala Harris. But it remains to be seen whether Musk’s money can help get more pro-Trump candidates over the finish line to make sure Republicans retain control of Congress.

In Michigan, Mike Rogers is the presumptive Republican nominee for the U.S. Senate race, but there’s a brutal fight on the Democratic side between lefty progressive Abdul El-Sayed and establishment favorite Haley Stevens. El-Sayed is leading 54% to 39%, according to a new poll from Emerson published Thursday.

In the Alaska race for U.S. Senate, Democratic challenger Mary Peltola is facing Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan. The latest polling shows that race is a toss-up.

In Iowa, Republican Joni Ernst is retiring, which has left an open Senate seat. Republican Ashley Hinson is facing off against Democrat Josh Turek. The latest polling has Hinson ahead 48% to 46% among likely voters, according to the Des Moines Register.

The U.S. Senate race in Maine was thrown into chaos after Democrat Graham Platner was forced out over sexual assault allegations, which he denies. Troy Jackson was elected to become the new Democratic candidate last week, and he will face off against Republican incumbent Susan Collins in November. Jackson’s presence in the race is so new that it’s hard to take any poll at face value yet, though he’s performed about even with Collins in some of the latest surveys.

Part of Musk’s efforts to influence the 2024 election was to hand out $1 million checks to potential voters. Musk largely escaped consequences for literally trying to buy votes, though Wisconsin could still bring criminal charges if authorities decide to bring them. We wouldn’t be surprised to see similar shenanigans in the midterms, though there’s no word yet on whether Musk has any plans along those lines.

Musk wouldn’t even need to offer $1 million to be effective at influencing elections. All you’d need is to hyper-target reliably Republican areas with much smaller sums of money.

Trump’s approval ratings are in the toilet, which means many Republicans might just stay home. Would you make the time to vote if you were promised a few thousand or even a few hundred dollars? Many Americans likely would, even if it’s illegal. But Musk proved you can do blatantly illegal shit if you’re rich enough and hedge with the right words.

On paper, Musk wasn’t paying for votes. He was paying for people to sign a petition promoting free speech or against activist judges. And it wouldn’t be a shock if he tried some version of that again.

news.title: Would a Janet Mills endorsement help Troy Jackson in the Maine Senate race?
news.text:
Gov. Janet Mills on Tuesday stopped short of endorsing her party’s nominee, Democrat Troy Jackson, for U.S. Senate. 

Instead, Mills focused on her party’s mission: giving the old Bean Boot to Susan Collins, the five-term Republican incumbent.

“Susan Collins is vulnerable and she should be defeated,” Mills told reporters after an event in Dresden in which she declared this upcoming weekend “Wild Blueberry Weekend.”

Mills didn’t explicitly rule out a future endorsement of Jackson. Such moments are usually done in coordination with a campaign, and the governor said she had not yet spoken to Jackson since he became the nominee last week.

But the episode begs the question: Would Jackson benefit from a Mills endorsement? 

Mills was forced out of the Democratic Senate primary in April. She was trailing in the polls and lagged in fundraising. And recent polling shows her favorability ratings underwater. But the midterms are an all-hands-on-deck moment for Democrats looking to defeat Collins.

Jackson’s campaign didn’t address whether he would seek or accept Mills’ endorsement when asked about it on Wednesday.

“Troy worked with Governor Mills to pass some of the most progressive abortion rights legislation in the country,” a campaign spokesperson said in a written statement. “This campaign is going to take everyone coming together to beat Susan Collins, and we’re confident Mainers will do just that.”

This week, Jackson was endorsed by former Vice President Kamala Harris.

A New York Times/Portland Press Herald/Siena poll conducted in June, when Graham Platner was the Democratic nominee, showed Mills’ favorability at minus-8 percentage points. That was worse than Collins, who was also underwater at minus-2 points.

That poll didn’t test Jackson’s favorability, since at that point he had lost the governor’s primary and Platner had not yet dropped out of the Senate race. But a separate survey by the University of New Hampshire Survey Center earlier this month showed Jackson’s favorability above water — at plus-5 points. 

Despite these ratings, Jackson’s campaign statement at least left the door open to accepting an endorsement by focusing on areas in which Mills and Jackson agreed when he was president of the Maine Senate. 

In addition to expanding abortion access in 2023, Jackson helped Mills broaden the MaineCare program right after she took office in 2019. And they worked together to provide free meals to public school students and bolster the childcare industry here.

But Jackson’s campaign statement also marks a shift in tone from Democratic gubernatorial primary, when he sought to distance himself from the governor. (Mills endorsed Hannah Pingree, the eventual Democratic nominee, in that race.)

Mills and Jackson had numerous policy disagreements during the latter’s six years as senate president.

During a televised debate in May, Jackson noted that Mills had vetoed 40 of his bills. He pointed to a specific measure to limit the price of prescription drugs.

“She said big pharma was going to sue us,” Jackson said, adding that a similar measure has since been implemented in Colorado. “Big pharma always sues. That’s their business model.”

Jackson also supported sweeping bills to recognize tribal sovereignty. Mills opposed those broad efforts in favor of more incremental reforms — a position that infuriated progressives.

Jackson also sought to expand the power of labor unions, including bills to benefit farmworkers. He sponsored a bill that would have made arbitration binding on wages and other issues during an impasse in contract negotiations. But those efforts were often opposed by the state’s chief executive, who has been the subject of several labor complaints from state unions.

There were also regular disagreements over state budgets. Jackson wanted higher spending levels, given historic state revenues. But Mills worried about an economic downturn and urged her party, which controls both chambers, to show fiscal restraint. 

While some of those disagreements happened behind closed doors, they occasionally spilled into public. So much so that in 2021, a progressive political action committee, Run Troy Run, tried to draft Jackson to run against Mills in the 2022 governor’s race.

Jackson dismissed the effort, and endorsed Mills, his party’s leader in the state.
news.summary: The governor suspended her own senate campaign in April and polling has shown her favorability rating underwater.

news.title: Jon Stewart Blasts Democratic Leaders For Not Working Out This 'Easily Rectifiable' Problem
news.text:
Jon Stewart is calling out a lack of leadership in the Democratic Party as the clock ticks down to the midterm elections. (Watch in the clip below.)

On the latest episode of his “Weekly Show” podcast, Stewart reacted to recent reporting from The New York Times outlining internal chaos as $2 million of debt looms over the Democratic National Committee, leaving Republicans with a massive cash advantage.

“When you’re in a position for a wave election and the article that comes out is, the guy in charge of the logistics of it is throwing phones at people and is broke ... that feels like the story of like, ‘How I Ended Up On Skid Row,’” Stewart quipped.

He later added, “The Democrats feel like, ‘You know, we have a great opportunity here.’ And then they just go around the meeting asking for ideas of how to fuck it up.”

The Times’ description of DNC Chair Ken Martin throwing a phone at a junior aide, a move that reportedly sparked a human resources complaint, was part of a story detailing “paranoia” and “rising anxiety” among Democrats about the state of the party’s fundraising apparatus heading into November.

Martin’s time as DNC head has been met with party backlash due to weak fundraising on his watch and his release of an unfinished draft of an autopsy on the 2024 election loss, reversing his earlier stance against such a move.

His tenure has sparked debate within the party, with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) emphasizing his “full support” for Martin, and others, such as Kamala Harris’ 2024 campaign finance chair Rufus Gifford, declaring that there’s “no saving” his chairmanship.

Stewart joked that the party is trying to understand how to “snatch defeat” from “the jaws of victory.”

“And the problem with it is it seems so easily rectifiable,” he continued.

“But it is, when you don’t know the difference between Chuck Schumer and [Zohran] Mamdani, and you don’t know how to square that circle, and you don’t have anybody who can unify that message —”

He went on, “Like, how the fuck they haven’t come up with their own ‘Contract for America,’ or even if it’s a gimmick to centralize the general complaints of a public thirsty for some actionable ideas and leadership, is malpractice bordering on criminal.”

Stewart argued that while infighting is necessary, there should be “outfighting,” as well.

Instead, the socialist moment was merely the logical culmination of years of boutique radicalism within the Democratic aristocracy — the ossified leadership of Chuck Schumer, Nancy Pelosi, Elizabeth Warren, Kamala Harris, and Hakeem Jeffries, along with the aging Black Caucus, the incoherent Squad, the DEI crowd, the open-border zealots, and the radical greens.

Democrats As Dr. Frankenstein

And that should be — everyone should take note of that, on both levels, that they're not going to let up, and they should not, and we should not."

After four months of rioting in 2020 — which left 25 people dead and 1,500 law enforcement officers injured, inflicted $2 billion in damage, and saw a police precinct, a federal courthouse, and an iconic church set ablaze — who gave the perpetrators a pass, with 14,000 arrests followed by few convictions and fewer jailings?

The Frankenstein Monster Awakens

So the socialists and communists did not really hijack the party. Rather, these youthful radicals were spawned and nurtured by aged Democrats. They became irate over their impotence and loss of influence — and simply upgraded the methods and message of their elders.

The upper-middle-class Mamdanis, Pikers, and AOCs did not storm the party parapets but were invited in by a party that had already radicalized itself — amid its hatred of Trump, its growing estrangement from the majority of the American people, and its fury at becoming increasingly powerless without the White House, Congress, or the Supreme Court.

Socialists did not lower the bar for extremism; establishment Democrats had already destroyed that standard altogether.

Given all that, the Democratic Socialists of America scarcely had to be invented.

After a decade of establishment Democrats destroying norms and traditions, deliberately dividing us by race, seeking to eliminate life-giving fossil fuels, and trying to implement dangerous crackpot ideas like critical race theory, critical legal theory, no cash bail, and defunding the police, the only change is that the now-electrified socialist monsters have awakened. In their place arose a cohort of upper-middle-class, degreed but otherwise poorly educated white urbanites, furious that their empty university certificates, student debt, inflated sense of self, and precious titles and jobs — but low salaries — had not delivered the affluent lifestyles enjoyed by lawyers, doctors, stockbrokers, and other professionals in their urban circles who had real jobs.

For both groups, anger was fed by envy of others with more stuff and by furor at a Middle America that plowed ahead, ignoring both their supposed talents and their hyped plight. America will soon see how this insanity works out.

news.title: Young Dems’ radicalism threatens to doom their party in midterms — and beyond
news.text:
Energy is the word of the day, week, month, and years to come in the Democratic Party.

As progressive challengers take on — and often dispatch — establishment figures in primaries from sea to shining sea, their movement has earned rounds of applause for its vitality.

Former President Barack Obama, for example, has deemed New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani an “extraordinary talent.”

Ex-Vice President Kamala Harris has praised him for “bringing people in,” marveling that it’s “so powerful.”

Three far-left congressional candidates endorsed by the mayor prevailed in the Big Apple last month; Graham Platner retired Gov. Janet Mills before primary day in Maine and has been replaced on the ballot by a fellow traveler; and Abdul El-Sayed has gone from underdog to favorite in his race against Haley Stevens in Michigan.

Energy, momentum, dynamism: whatever you want to call it, this faction has it in spades, in large part thanks to the young voters who have propelled them to victory — and ushered in an entirely new era for their party.

A new Manhattan Institute survey of 1,121 likely voters across the country leaves little doubt as to whether this is a blip on the radar or a taste of the courses to come.

Among left-leaning respondents between the age of 18 and 34, 67% identify as democratic socialists.

Among those between 35 and 49, that figure drops, but is still 56%.

Even among 50 to 64-year-olds, 45% are reaching for their hammers and sickles.

The forecast for Team Blue is red — with a string of inevitable electoral disappointments.

Because what’s popular among the ascendant majority in the Democratic base is not among the American majority that decides elections.

“There is a reason why Republicans nationwide are licking their chops,” observed CNN data guru Harry Enten during one recent segment about the Democratic Socialists of America’s dismal net favorability rating of negative 27 points.

Sixty-six percent of Democrats have a positive view of “socialism” more generally, up from 50% in 2010.

Among the public at large, though, that figure has hardly changed at all: 29% in 2010, 30% now.

In short, Democrats keep moving further left, even as America stays where it is.

The Manhattan Institute poll yielded still more bad news for Democrats.

On a wide variety of discrete policy issues, Americans continue to embrace a common sense and reject the DSA approach.

Fifty-three percent want to “crack down on waste, fraud, and abuse” within the welfare system, while just 31% want to “make it easier to eligible people to receive welfare benefits.”

Sixty-five percent identify the objective of government assistance has “making sure everyone has a basic minimum,” rather than “reducing the gap between the rich and the poor” (21%).

And even though the Democrats have long since renounced Bill Clinton’s efforts at triangulation, the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act he signed into law in 1996 remains enormously popular.

The DSA’s calls for the abolition of police, prisons, and borders, on the other hand, are underwater by 72, 67, and 64 points, respectively.

This should be a banner year for Democrats. RealClearPolitics pegs President Trump’s net approval rating at nearly negative 18.

Yet most generic ballot polls suggest Democrats are only outpacing their Republican opponents by a few points — some even say they’re all knotted up.

In Maine, Sen. Susan Collins has gained the upper hand since Platner dropped out and subsequently replaced by a less charismatic copycat.

In Michigan, one recent survey showed Republican Mike Rogers whooping El-Sayed by double digits.

And per Quinnipiac, more Americans (46%) view Democrats as too extreme than see Republicans (40%) as the same.

Insulated from reality by their media allies, Democrats tend to blame disappointing Election Days on their messaging, SuperPACs, disinformation, less-than-compelling candidates — everything but their ideas.

But if they underperform in the House and all but forfeit winnable Senate seats during the midterm cycle of Donald Trump’s second term, they’ll have a verdict on just how much their precious enthusiasm is worth outside of the confines of deep blue cities and low-turnout primary contests.

Just don’t expect them to take it to heart; the “energy” is working against them.
news.summary: Democrats will soon have a verdict on just how much their precious enthusiasm is worth outside of the confines of deep blue cities and low-turnout primary contests.

news.title: The Teamsters betrayed their own workers — and Republicans fell for it again
news.text:
The Teamsters stay in lock step with the rest of Big Labor. In the 2024 election cycle, House Democrats received far more labor contributions than House Republicans. Senate Democrats received the overwhelming share as well. The United Auto Workers endorsed Kamala Harris for president. The AFL-CIO, representing 60 unions and 12.5 million workers, unanimously endorsed Kamala Harris in July 2024. This came after they had already made the earliest presidential endorsement in AFL-CIO history to back Joe Biden in June 2023. It’s no different with the teachers’ unions. The National Education Association raised roughly $27 million through its PAC for the 2024 election cycle, with roughly 98% of contributions going to Democrats.

Union dues flow to union PACs. Union PACs flow to Democrats. The leadership of these organizations has traded worker advocacy for a subscription model that funds their political allies, and the machine runs the same way regardless of what Republicans do or what rank-and-file members actually want. Time and again, the organization overrides the preferences of the very workers it claims to represent.

The Ohio endorsement puts this on full display at exactly the right moment. Republicans hold the Senate majority. Republicans control the House. Trump needs to have a Republican Congress to deliver on his agenda. If there were ever a moment when the organization might recalibrate, extend an olive branch, or at least consider rewarding members of the governing coalition who have moved toward them on trade and manufacturing policy, this would be it. Instead, they endorsed a Democrat in a critical state, against a Republican-controlled Senate, the only body capable of advancing legislation that union leadership claims to support.

When union leaders demanded policy concessions from Republicans in exchange for cooperation or neutrality, some Republicans obliged. I have been around DC enough to know what happens next: the concessions get made, and the money and endorsements go to Democrats anyway. A Republican who bends on policy to earn organizational support reaps what they sow.

The rank-and-file members who voted for Trump, who support Republican candidates with their own money, and who disagree with the political choices their leadership makes on their behalf deserve better. Many of these workers backed Trump and Republican policies at the ballot box. The organization’s own polling confirmed the gap between membership preferences and leadership decisions. Yet the organization continues to act against those preferences with dues-funded PACs and endorsements. The conversation about workers’ interests belongs with those workers directly, not with institutions that have directed 92 to 97 cents of every political dollar to Democrats for thirty-plus years.

REPUBLICANS ARE ABOUT TO MAKE A NEW BILLION-DOLLAR UNION IN COLLEGE SPORTS WORLD

Take this endorsement for what it is: A reminder that union leadership is not a constituency to be won over through policy compromise. The money, the endorsements, and the organizing power will go to the Democrat machine when it matters, even when the membership clearly leans the other way. Republicans who want to compete for workers should advance policies that grow paychecks and expand opportunity, and they should stop treating national union leadership as votes that can be won.

Thirty years of data already answered that question. This Ohio endorsement just confirmed it.

Gene Hamilton is Senior Advisor for the Coalition to Protect American Workers.

news.title: No vacation, no excuses: The 82% winner sitting on the Senate floor
news.text:
According to results of a new survey conducted for Tea Party Patriots Action by McLaughlin & Associates, overwhelming majorities of voters — including strong majorities of Republicans, Democrats, independents, those who support President Donald Trump, those who oppose Trump, liberals, moderates, conservatives, those who voted for Trump in 2024, those who voted for Democratic candidate Kamala Harris in 2024, whites, African-Americans, Hispanics, married people, single people, men, and women — agree that “only United States citizens should be allowed to vote in elections for U.S. President, U.S. Senate, and U.S. House.”

Among all voters surveyed, 82% agree with that statement, compared to just 12% who disagree.

This should not shock anyone. It’s common sense.

Not surprisingly, since such a large percentage believe only U.S. citizens should be allowed to vote in federal elections, similar majorities of the same groups agree that “proof of United States citizenship should be required to register to vote in American elections”: fully 78% among all voters agree with that statement, compared to just 16% who disagree.

Voters are similarly supportive of requiring that they produce a photo ID before casting a ballot — in this most recent survey, 78% agree that “voters should be required to show a photo ID when casting a ballot.”

Again, this should not shock anyone. It’s common sense.

And it follows previous surveys over the last few years showing essentially the same thing — vast majorities of voters, across virtually all partisan, ideological, and demographic lines, agree that only U.S. citizens should be allowed to vote in federal elections, and that proof of citizenship should be required to register to vote in U.S. elections, and that photo ID should be required to cast a ballot.

Perhaps more to the point right now, the new survey shows that voters want the Senate to continue working to pass the bill — by 56%-34%, they chose “the United States Senate should continue to work to pass the bill before this year’s elections” over “the United States Senate should give up on passing the bill this year.”

Republicans have an issue that cuts 82-12 their way, and the majority of voters want them to pass the bill before the November elections. That’s an opportunity, served up on a silver platter.

Thune and his GOP colleagues could take advantage of it by bringing the budget resolution to the floor that just passed the House. It contains a $10 billion fund and an opening for elements of the SAVE America Act that have overwhelming public support.

Bringing the resolution to the floor would force Democrats on the defensive. They’d face a choice — vote in support of their constituents’ desires or be required to explain to their constituents why they oppose such a commonsense measure.

Georgia’s Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-GA), for instance, should be required to cast a vote on the measure. If he wants to represent his constituents’ desires on the matter, he’ll vote for it. But the extreme radical left-wing base of his party expects him to oppose the measure — and as he runs for reelection, he’s chosen to cater to that radical base.

Decisions have consequences. Ossoff should pay a political price for his decision to cater to his radical base.

It’s not just Ossoff. By bringing the resolution up for consideration, Thune could use the attention-focusing aspect of debate on the Senate floor to make Democrat candidates for the Senate in Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire, North Carolina, Ohio, and Texas explain to their voters why they don’t support a measure that their voters do, overwhelmingly.

In politics, you win by going on offense and taking control of the argument — and you make your opponent talk about the things you want to talk about. In this case, Senate Republicans have the opportunity to force their own campaign debates — and the campaign debates of GOP candidates who want to join them in the Senate — onto the topic of proof of citizenship to register and photo ID to vote.

NON-CITIZEN VOTING IS REAL. WE DON’T NEED THE SAVE AMERICA ACT TO CLEAN ROLLS

The SAVE America Act should be passed by the Senate because it would be good for the country. It would help alleviate the erosion of confidence in the integrity of our election systems by making it clear to voters that government officials take election security seriously.

Republicans should seize this moral high ground by staying in town long enough to consider and pass the budget resolution with the key elements of the SAVE America Act. That would be good for the country, and good for themselves.

Jenny Beth Martin is chairman of Tea Party Patriots Action.

news.title: Bernie Moreno explains his Fauci F-bomb amid a rising tide of political profanity
news.text:
Secrets suspects that Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-OH) spoke for most of the Republicans present when he went blue with rage.

“It was about six years ago today that I decided I’m going to give up my businesses, sell them all, run for office, run through the United States Senate,” he told the retired scientist.

“Here I am sitting in front of you six years later saying, who the f*** do you think you were for doing that?”

Studies suggest the use of expletives in politics is becoming more common. Academics believe it represents an attempt to connect with voters with a display of authenticity.

But Moreno told Secrets that there was nothing calculated about his words.

“It was pent-up anger at a guy who did enormous harm to many Americans, especially children,” he said.

“Not planned as I work really hard not to swear out of respect for the office and the institution,” Moreno added. “But … he is a truly despicable human being, and that was the visceral reaction I had to his pleading the Fifth and not looking at those in the gallery he harmed… hiding behind a scumbag attorney.”

Moreno also asked Fauci to face people in the room who believed they had been harmed by mandates and closures during the pandemic response, but Fauci refused.

Yet the senator’s comments were not the only example on Wednesday.

Trey Yingst, a Fox News reporter, had to do some on-air censoring of a conversation that he had just had with President Donald Trump about Iran’s overnight strikes on U.S. facilities.

“We’re going to beat the effing s out of them,” is how the reporter rather carefully put it.

And Secrets apologizes to any readers who were offended by a quote in Wednesday’s newsletter, where we were asking sources whether Pete Hegseth was safe in his role at the Pentagon, amid growing criticism from Republican senators.

“If you think the president gives a f*** about what Thom Tillis or Joni Ernst think about Hegseth, it’s a major misread,” said one.

What does it all mean? Apart from that, we could be heading for a national asterisk shortage.

Dr. Joseph Phillips, a lecturer in Politics at Cardiff University, recently published data showing that the use of expletives was on the rise in presidential politics.

“It used to be rare for presidents, even as candidates, to swear in official remarks,” Phillips said. “Woodrow Wilson broke the profanity seal in 1919, recounting a time where he made a ‘conspicuous *ss of himself.’ Since then, presidents, their seconds-in-command, and presidential hopefuls have used profanity at least 692 times.”

And it is accelerating, with 87% of all profanity coming in the past 10 years. Some 78% of all uses have come from two politicians: Trump and Joe Biden.

“While Biden heavily relied on ‘damn,’ Trump’s usage of profanity has been more varied, introducing ‘b******,’ ‘b***’, ‘bulls***’, and ‘f***’ into the presidential vocabulary,” he said.

Connoisseurs of profanity will note that there is one rather Germanic boundary still to be crossed.

Secrets wonders what that will take. Maybe Kamala Harris declaring for 2028?

It’s all entertainment now

Should we be surprised that some of the most nuanced analysis of the Fauci hearing comes from TMZ?

Harvey Levin, founder of the channel, used his platform to offer his thoughts. And they are complicated. At one point, he explains that as a gay man, he knew many men who died horrible deaths of AIDS in the 1980s, and that Fauci was instrumental in accelerating treatments that saved lives.

Anyway, there are two parts to his commentary:

“I have problems with the way the CDC handled COVID. I think that they did damage to children, to adults, and I don’t think they did it maliciously. I think they did it because they were using their judgment and were overprotective, and I think at times overstated things … things they said they knew but really didn’t, and I have personal problems with the way that COVID was handled.”

But is Sen. Rand Paul (R-KY) the right person to be getting to the bottom of the questions?

“I mean, he has said now over a period of years he wants Anthony Fauci in a jail cell. He has said it out loud. He wants him in a jail cell. That’s the point of this hearing. That’s why they’re doing this. They want to take something that Anthony Fauci says and then claim it amounts to perjury, and they want to prosecute him, they want to convict him, and they want to throw him in prison. That’s the point of this hearing…”

“There are things they could certainly ask him, but he can’t answer because if he answers, it doesn’t matter what he says … You know, if you can prosecute somebody for fricking seashells on the beach shore, then you could certainly prosecute somebody for what they say in a congressional hearing, and that’s the climate we’re in.”

It is well worth watching the whole thing, then reflecting on where politics is today and the best ways to cover it. (As TMZ leans more into political coverage.) Plus, whether the public is being well served by its elected politicians.

Lunchtime reading
