news.title: How the Big Beautiful Bill became law: Trump the closer
news.text:
He told the Washington Examiner, “A lot of people get weak-kneed when the president calls, and he usually has completed the transaction within a couple of minutes.”

HOW THE BIG BEAUTIFUL BILL BECAME LAW: READ MORE FROM THE WASHINGTON EXAMINER’S 10-PART SERIES

House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-LA) said Trump “was our best closer.” 

John McLaughlin, a Trump pollster, said getting the bill done by Independence Day was an ambitious goal and the president “willed” it to happen.

House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Jason Smith (R-MO) said Trump was engaged throughout the bill’s ups and downs: “I can’t tell you how many times the president called me.”

Republicans interviewed for this series said Trump understood the politics of extending the 2017 tax cuts he signed into law during his first term. If the reductions weren’t renewed, Republicans said people and the economy would suffer because taxes would go up roughly $4 trillion over 10 years. But Trump was well aware that just extending the tax reductions wouldn’t be enough to get the 2025 measure over the finish line, especially with Republicans having small majorities in the House and Senate.

The scope of the big beautiful bill was enormous, addressing school choice, the border, the military, spectrum, Medicaid, and many other items. Scalise told the Washington Examiner that 11 committee chairmen worked on the legislation.

But the meat and potatoes of the legislation was taxes, and Trump realized there needed to be some new bells and whistles.

At a 2024 campaign stop in Nevada, home to many service workers, Trump rattled Kamala Harris’s campaign by promising no taxes on tips if elected. A couple months later, Harris endorsed the idea and Trump called her a “copycat.”

Trump doubled down by promising no taxes on overtime and Social Security, and those concepts were subsequently put in the big beautiful bill. 

There were other new ideas, such as the “Trump Accounts,” 401(k)-like retirement savings program for children, which Bessent and Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX) pushed for. Cruz has called the creation of the accounts “Trump’s New Deal” and said the accounts will be transformative for decades to come.

Still, passing the behemoth measure was never going to be easy.

Trump wields his endorsement power

The biggest weapon Trump wielded to get the votes was his coveted endorsements in primaries. If you crossed Trump, there was a significant risk he would endorse, or recruit, a GOP challenger. While a few have survived Republican primaries against a Trump-backed opponent, such cases are rare.

Trump and Republican leaders could only afford a few GOP defections in both the House and the Senate. And there was a lot of squawking from a couple dozen GOP and conservatives. The centrists were wary of the bill’s Medicaid spending reforms, while Freedom Caucus members insisted on massive deficit reduction.

TRUMP ENDORSEMENT TRACKER: HERE’S WHO THE PRESIDENT HAS PICKED IN GOP MIDTERM ELECTION PRIMARIES

After the Senate barely passed the big beautiful bill, Trump turned his attention to the always unpredictable House. After countless conversations in person and on the phone, Trump ended up getting all but two House Republicans to vote for the bill.

One no vote was Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY), a frequent target of Trump’s ire. Massie had survived prior primary challenges, but Trumpworld this cycle went all in and recruited a strong candidate to take him on in 2026.

Massie, a libertarian lawmaker who has served in Congress since 2012, regularly bucked the White House, and Trump wanted him gone — especially after he rejected the president’s top legislative priority. Massie, who relishes taking on the GOP establishment, reportedly got tired of Trump’s incessant public attacks.

Toward the end of the debate last summer, the Wall Street Journal reported that Massie agreed to vote for a pivotal procedural measure that allowed the final version of the big beautiful bill to advance under the condition that Trump would ease up on him. Trump later renewed his criticisms of Massie, who in May lost to Trump’s endorsed candidate, Ed Gallrein.

The other no vote was Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-PA), a former FBI agent who represents a battleground district. Unlike Massie, Fitzpatrick is usually a reliable vote for GOP leaders and doesn’t engage in skirmishes with the president. He rejected the final bill because of its Medicaid and energy tax provisions.

Asked what he was feeling when he cast his vote, Fitzpatrick told the Washington Examiner, “Standing by my district, that’s a good feeling, it’s not a bad feeling. If you fear people in this town, then yes, it’s anxiety-provoking. I don’t work for anybody here.”

Fitzpatrick had voted for the initial House bill, but said the Senate made the measure worse.

At last week’s White House Correspondents’ Association dinner, Trump said nice things about Fitzpatrick at one point during his speech. But he did note he’d like a “couple more votes… That’s okay. On occasion, he chose a little independence.”

President refs fights between House and Senate

There were many intraparty fights among Republicans on Capitol Hill about the big beautiful bill. The House and Senate clashed on state and local taxes, energy tax credits, and the price tag of the legislation.

But one of the most significant battles, and the first out of the gate, was whether Republicans should pass Trump’s 2025 legislative wish list in one or two pieces of legislation.

House Republicans strongly favored one, while the Senate GOP was partial to two. Republican senators made the case for passing one reconciliation bill focused on border security and then moving on to the more complicated issue of extending the tax cuts. Trump initially went back and forth as congressional leaders lobbied him.

Bessent said some Republicans on Capitol Hill were advocating for three or four reconciliation bills. 

Ways and Means Committee Chairman Jason Smith (R-MO) repeatedly said the two-bill approach wouldn’t work. He said he told Scalise, “No way… I won’t stand for it.”

Scalise warned Bessent that unless there was one big bill, the chances of passing the second were less than 50%. 

Grover Norquist, head of the Americans for Tax Reform, said that “all the grownups wanted one.”

Their rationale was simple: There were going to be enticements that lawmakers liked, as well as controversial spending reductions. The candy and the spinach had to go together. Moreover, House Republican leaders wanted as much time as possible for people to feel the benefits of the legislation — and that meant one bill cleared by the summer of 2025.

Senators countered that it would be better to put points on the board and deal with the tax component later. After all, they said, the tax cuts weren’t going to expire until the end of 2025.

The House ended up winning over the president.

In an interview, Senate Majority Leader John Thune recounted how Trump relayed his ultimate decision. The South Dakota Republican said Trump sent him a long text explaining why one was better than two.

“It will be glamorous,” Thune quoted Trump’s text, adding the president used a lot of capital letters and exclamation marks in his message.

The White House team mobilizes

When James Braid needs a boost, he goes straight to the Marlboro Reds. And he burned them by the packful during last summer to flip members of Congress into voting yes for Trump’s big beautiful bill.

Braid, the White House director of legislative affairs, White House deputy chief of staff James Blair, and Vice President JD Vance formed the tip of the spear with Trump, the hand that drove it home.

During the final week of the debate, “The Jameses” practically lived on Capitol Hill, strategizing with Vance in his ceremonial Senate office, working the phones, and, when necessary, catching a few minutes of sleep on the floor of House Homeland Security Committee Chairman Andrew Garbarino’s (R-NY) Capitol Hill hideaway office.

On June 29, the pair traveled out to Trump National Golf Club in Sterling, Virginia, for a private meeting with the president, Sens. Katie Britt (R-AL) and Eric Schmitt (R-MO), both champions of the bill, as well as Sen. Ron Johnson (R-WI), and Rick Scott (R-FL), who were skeptical of it. The sitdown lasted several hours, taking place in a room on the club’s second floor, “looking out onto the president’s golf course,” focused solely on cutting an “agreement” for a motion to proceed, according to White House insiders.

Trump played golf before the meeting, personally lobbying Sen. Rand Paul (R-KY). Paul had criticized the bill over federal debt concerns and agreed to discuss his opposition over a round with the president at the request of the late South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham.

Hours later, the Senate passed the motion to proceed, allowing the bill to move to the floor for official debate, at which point things got even tougher.

“In the early part of that week, there was a lot of controversy and frustration in the Senate Republican conference,” Braid told the Washington Examiner. “The effort had secured the support of most everybody but certain holdouts and defeated a bunch of amendments that would have struck out portions of that agreement.”

Tuesday night, July 1, was “touch and go.” The entire White House Office of Legislative Affairs Senate team, joined by Blair and Braid, faced a major problem: the Senate was still one vote shy of passage in Vance’s Senate office.

Even though Sen. Susan Collins (R-ME) had voted yes on the motion to proceed, she was still a hard no on the overall bill alongside Paul, and Sen. Thom Tillis (R-NC). 

Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-AK) was waving red flags over changes to Medicaid funding, leading Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-AK), Blair, and Braid to broker a deal that offered generous Medicaid funding for the state of Alaska. The trio got the green light from Trump and managed to bring Murkowski on board.

Later that day, the Senate passed the bill, with Vance casting the tiebreaking vote. 

Braid recalled heading home, taking a shower, and immediately heading back to the House, where some Republicans were up in arms over the Senate’s changes.

White House legislative affairs staffers were able to earn the support of most Republicans but identified some two-dozen House Freedom Caucus members who would require the president’s personal touch to vote yes. The president has referred to that group as the “3 o’clock caucus” because he had to call them in the middle of the night to sway them.

“President Trump didn’t sleep for those two days,” Braid recounted. “He was checking in every half hour to 45 minutes, getting updates and talking to people and moving guys.”

Trump’s quandary on Planned Parenthood

Trump faced a dilemma: Anti-abortion groups and lawmakers wanted the big beautiful bill to include a ban on Medicaid dollars for groups such as Planned Parenthood.

The issue was on the agenda at a White House meeting with Trump, chief of staff Susie Wiles, Blair, House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA), and Thune.

Polling showed that adding language that “defunded Planned Parenthood” was a poison pill, according to a person familiar. The fear was that Democrats would use the issue during the 2026 midterm cycle to hammer vulnerable Republicans in House districts that the GOP needed to win, similar to their success during the 2022 midterm cycle after Roe v. Wade was overturned.

Trump, who indirectly helped the fall of Roe by getting three conservative justices to the Supreme Court in his first term, thought abortion was a political loser for his party. But if Republicans didn’t address the matter, conservatives could withhold their support and torpedo the overall bill.

Trump’s reluctance was relayed by Johnson to anti-abortion and pro-family groups. Their response was clear: not acceptable. Some members of the House Republican Conference were also uncomfortable with doing nothing.

Johnson, whom many anti-abortion groups have championed as a hero, subsequently told Trump that defunding Planned Parenthood had to be included in the legislation. The president listened.

Anti-abortion groups, however, weren’t leaving anything to chance. They pressured Republican lawmakers to follow through with defunding Planned Parenthood. It was a multi-pronged strategy that paid off, with a catch.

More than 150 anti-abortion groups, including Students for Life and Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America, rallied on Capitol Hill in late March 2025. They also sent letters to members of Congress connecting defunding “Big Abortion” to Elon Musk’s efforts through the Department of Government Efficiency to trim the federal budget.

“We felt very strongly that, given the massive turnout of voters of faith that made the 2024 victory possible, that it was absolutely critical that we achieve some significant progress on the life issue in the first year of Trump’s second term,” said Ralph Reed, chairman of the Faith and Freedom Coalition. “And in the absence of a judicial vacancy or some other legislative vehicle that was going to have to be in the tax cut bill.”

“We were not reticent about making that view known to both the White House and congressional Republican leaders,” Reed added.

Anti-abortion groups also traveled to states and congressional districts to make their case in the spring of 2025.

Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America won a public victory when Johnson promised to make sure the bill would “redirect funds away from big abortion and to federally qualified health centers,” at its April gala. That was the first time, at least in public, that Republican leadership was explicit on their Planned Parenthood strategy.

The next month, the group targeted key House members with over 3,300 constituent calls to their D.C. and district offices, as well as organized more than 183 pro-life legislators in 49 states, to send a letter to Republican leaders to defund Planned Parenthood.

There were also regular coalition meetings between multiple anti-abortion groups, according to Susan B. Anthony’s political communications director, Kelsey Pritchard.

“I think it could have blown up at any time, especially at the beginning,” Pritchard said of the work the groups did. “It was never inevitable. It was never like for sure that we were going to be able to do this because it hadn’t been done before.”

Their efforts proved somewhat successful, fulfilling a goal decades in the making.

The legislation defunding Planned Parenthood would pass in the House on May 22, 2025. But in the Senate, anti-abortion leaders saw their victory stripped to a one-year funding ban amid concern that Senate Parliamentarian Elizabeth MacDonough could toss the House language because it would violate budget reconciliation rules. 

On June 30, 2025, MacDonough allowed the one-year defunding provision to stay in the measure.

“The Senate, in our opinion, negotiated with itself,” said Kristi Hamrick, vice president of media and policy for Students for Life of America. “In the past, the parliamentarian had liked or been amenable to the idea of one year. Well, the parliamentarian’s advice has been ignored in the past.”

Penny Nance, CEO and president of Concerned Women for America, said she was disappointed with the parliamentarian’s ruling and also confused about what it meant.

“If it were appropriate for one year, logically, I think it would also have been appropriate for 10 years, and because we don’t know what logic she used to arrive at the decision, we don’t exactly know how to go back at it again for budget reconciliation in the future,” said Nance.

Students for Life, like many other groups, made their displeasure clear to Thune’s office and pressured Senate Republicans to challenge the parliamentarian’s ruling. Eventually, they called for MacDonough to be removed.

But experts claimed the Senate operates on precedent. In 2017, the parliamentarian advised that language temporarily defunding abortion did not meet the so-called Byrd rule requirements, requiring a 60-vote majority to pass as Republicans attempted to repeal Obamacare. Republicans back then moved forward with defunding Planned Parenthood, but it did not meet the 60-vote threshold.

In 2025, Republicans met with the parliamentarian to propose a 10-year moratorium on Planned Parenthood receiving federal reimbursements.

“My understanding is that the vibes in the room from the questions the parliamentarian was asking could not be answered as to exactly the budgetary consequences,” said Bill Hoagland, the senior vice president of the Bipartisan Policy Center.

Republicans scaled down the timeline to one year, and the provisions expired earlier this month.

“That would not have the same impact on access to care that it would if it had been a 10-year depletion of funding,” said Hoagland. “And so this really was a decision by Republicans not to press the issue going forward.”

Although it wasn’t the exact time length they wanted, anti-abortion groups touted their victory.

“Of course, we wanted it to be 10 years,” Pritchard said. “At the same time, we knew we had to operate within the realities and processes of the Senate, and it had never been done before. And so, we kept up the enthusiasm and the energy to get one year.”

Lauren Green contributed to this story.

Members of the Washington Examiner’s staff who have worked on this series over the past several months are Haris Alic, Hailey Bullis, Bob Cusack, Christian Datoc, James A. Downs, Gabrielle M. Etzel, Lauren Green, Zach Halaschak, Chris Irvine, Joseph Lawler, Naomi Lim, Maydeen Merino, Callie Patteson, Mabinty Quarshie, Samantha-Jo Roth, David Sivak, and Ramsey Touchberry.

news.title: Beshear’s pressure campaign on McConnell tests his 2028 political brand
news.text:
Republicans contend Beshear is abandoning the bipartisan image that has made him one of the Democratic Party’s most prominent governors in favor of rhetoric aimed at winning over progressive activists ahead of a possible presidential campaign.

“By promoting ghoulish conspiracy theories about Sen. McConnell’s health, Andy Beshear has essentially fed a feral animal, and when you feed that beast once, you can never stop feeding it or it will bite your hand off,” former Kentucky Republican Party communications director Tres Watson told the Washington Examiner.

Watson argued Beshear risked alienating moderate voters attracted to his “Clintonesque ‘I feel your pain'” brand while still not going “nearly far enough for the feral, terminally online Left.”

Kentucky Republican strategist TJ Litafik agreed, arguing that “taking shots at McConnell will generate national attention and play well with Democratic activists and primary voters who have spent years despising the senator,” but it also came at a risk.

“Kentuckians generally don’t like seeing someone’s age or health turned into a political opportunity, particularly when the target is an 84-year-old man who has represented the commonwealth for more than four decades, and who isn’t running again,” Litafik told the Washington Examiner. “If Beshear continues to push harder, it looks less like genuine concern and more like base opportunism.”

Democrats counter that Beshear is raising legitimate questions about whether Kentucky is being adequately represented while McConnell remains away from the Senate.“We get elected by the people. The people are the boss. I think Andy Beshear is showing great restraint and respect in what he’s saying,” former California Sen. Barbara Boxer said during an appearance on MS NOW this week.

Simultaneously, some Democrats have questioned Beshear’s strategy regarding McConnell when the senator’s absence from the Senate and inability to vote by proxy could undermine President Donald Trump’s agenda in Congress before November’s midterm elections, after which Republicans could lose control of one of the chambers.

“Conspiracy theories are fun and all, but if you care about counting votes in the Senate, it is far better to have McConnell MIA these days,” Democratic strategist Jim Manley, who was communications director for former Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, told the Washington Examiner.

Spokespeople for Beshear and the Kentucky Democratic Party did not respond to the Washington Examiner’s request for comment. But Democratic strategist Matt Bennett, a former top aide to then-President Bill Clinton, came to the governor’s defense.

“Beshear has an obligation to ensure that the people of Kentucky have a senator who is capable of representing them,” the Third Way executive vice president for public affairs told the Washington Examiner. “It’s not at all clear that they do, so what he’s doing is appropriate. I doubt it will have much impact on a presidential run, but showing some spine and leadership like this can only help him.”

Beshear’s strategy comes as Democrats will likely encounter more questions about concerns regarding former President Joe Biden‘s physical and mental acuity when he was seeking a second term in office amid the release of his latest memoir after November’s elections.

But for Kentucky Republican Party communications director Adam Hope, it is “hypocritical” for Beshear to “blow this situation [with McConnell] out of proportion after remaining largely silent” when Republicans expressed concerns about Biden’s very “obvious cognitive decline.”

“Gov. Beshear will undoubtedly continue issuing statements and sending strongly worded letters in an effort to elevate himself and his presidential ambitions, despite polling in the single digits,” Hope told the Washington Examiner.

To that end, support for a Beshear 2028 presidential campaign polls at an average of 3 percentage points, well behind the likes of former Vice President Kamala Harris, Gov. Gavin Newsom (D-CA), and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, whose share of the hypothetical Democratic primary vote registers in double digits, according to RealClearPolitics.

Regardless, Beshear is embarking on a 13-stop book tour next month to promote his new memoir, Go and Do Likewise, a potential precursor to a presidential campaign. Stops, for example, include cities in early-voting primary election states, such as Georgia, Michigan, and New Hampshire.

McConnell announced his decision to retire after seven terms in the Senate, during which time he became the chamber’s longest-serving majority leader, on his 83rd birthday in February.

WHAT LEGISLATION HAS MITCH MCCONNELL’S ABSENCE STALLED IN THE SENATE?

McConnell was hospitalized in Washington, D.C., on June 14 and has not been seen in public since, though his doctors wrote in a note accompanying this week’s statement that he is out of the hospital but has not been “medically cleared” to return to work in the Senate.

McConnell’s office did not respond to the Washington Examiner’s request for comment, but the senator wrote this week he was “working hard to get back to my full schedule of work in the Senate and in Kentucky, keeping up with intense physical therapy per my doctors’ orders.”

news.title: Will Left-Wing Democrats Reinvent the Party or Hurt Its Chances in November?
news.text:
To try and understand the fissures in the Democratic Party, I recently spoke by phone with Faiz Shakir, Bernie Sanders’s 2020 Presidential-campaign manager and founder of the media nonprofit More Perfect Union. During our conversation, which has been edited for length and clarity, we discussed why so many Democrats are angry at the Party establishment, whether the Party is in danger of losing seats in swing states, and whether progressives, like Bernie Sanders, were right to stick with Joe Biden until the end of his reëlection campaign.
What do you see as the main division within the Democratic Party right now, and does it feel new?
I think it’s intensified. The division is over the desire of candidates to take on concentrations of wealth and power, and their willingness and desire to take on corporate greed and corporate power in general. There are people who were born for it, or desire it, and they are the candidates who tend to be doing quite well at this moment. They’re the ones who understand that part of your job in public service is to stand up to the power of moneyed interests, and how critical it is to speak out on behalf of people living paycheck to paycheck. There is friction against others in the Party who would say we don’t need that kind of tension with the moneyed élite. We have to raise money from them, we have to coddle them, we have to have public-private partnerships with them, we have to make them feel nice, and be kind to them.
I’m not saying tonally you have to be mean, but you have to acknowledge that there is friction and tension if you’re going to fight for working-class communities right now.
Do you think progressives should be focussing on running these types of candidates in safe, Democratic areas and states, so that the caucus in the House and the Senate is more left-wing and pushes for more left-wing ideas? Or do you also think they need to be pushing these types of candidates across the map?
I certainly come at this from a desire for persuasion. And, in order to be persuasive, I do tend to think that the candidates who are going to perform best across the board clearly define their desire to address concentrations of wealth and power, and the issues around corporate greed. And, if they are defined in that way, they can succeed in the reddest parts of this country. I do tend to think those candidates should start to reflect their geographies a bit, if they’re doing it the right way. So a New York City candidate who’s doing this may look and sound different than a Montana candidate who’s doing this.
You hear people like Senator Sanders, and yourself, say that the common thread for winning in diverse places is fighting for working people on economic issues. But, with candidates like Abdul El-Sayed, in Michigan, or Francesca Hong, in Wisconsin, you see left-wing campaigns running on very liberal social platforms. For example, El-Sayed has gotten tripped up over questions about defunding the police. I’m curious how you see that tension.
Many candidates run on liberal social-justice platforms. I don’t think you’re wrong that there are elements of that in this wave of progressive candidates. But what often happens is people look at their tweets from six years ago and miss how they are campaigning right now.
Look at how different candidates are talking about ICE: some use the word “abolish,” some say “reform,” some say “move funding to different agencies.” Those are all part and parcel of what I was suggesting—that you are attuned to the geographies in which you’re representing, and you are close to the people you’re representing. If you go talk to a lot of these working-class people, they are three-dimensional human beings. They know when somebody is being honest and levelling with them. And I see in a lot of these progressive candidates that, while they may have views on things that don’t one hundred per cent align with every working-class person in their district, there is a benefit because people understand the candidate is telling them what they really believe. And there’s points for honesty.
I thought you were saying that there was some need for candidates to change their pitch based on where they are running, though.
When you’re in Montana, the issues of housing play out a bit differently than the housing issues of New York City, right? The density of renters in New York City is very high. Montana, obviously, they’re going through tenant unions; they have their own issues, but there are a lot of people being squeezed out of their opportunity to own their own homes. I’m just arguing that economic justice, the way in which you talk about those affordability crises, will have geographic dimensions to them that matter to your relatability.
I see, so the issue is not that you need to moderate or change your pitch on social issues, depending on where you’re running.
Well, I agree with that, too. So if you’re running in Montana, you’re running in Idaho, you’re running in Ohio, I do think that a good candidate who is trying to appeal to the working class has to be aware of what the attitudinal views are of the community, and the candidate has to be interested in them and want to have a conversation about them. What are their views on trans kids? How’s the community feeling about immigration raids?
Darializa Chevalier is one of the most interesting candidates, and what people still miss about her is that she ran in a district that included Columbia University, and you and I both know what happened there: a ton of free-speech-restriction efforts from the Trump Administration, and Columbia students taken by ICE. And I think what Chevalier captured was a feeling of what that community was actually going through better than Adriano Espaillat, the incumbent congressman.
Her positive comments on communism may not have helped the argument that she cared about free speech.
[Laughs.] Well, you know, everyone’s their own unique candidate, let’s put it that way. It’s not to say that anybody who wins is perfect; there are no gods and prophets in this industry. It’s just about who has some sense of integrity and a willingness to fight. And this is what, in my view, it’s all boiling down to. Integrity and convictions of really giving a damn about those who aren’t élite, rich, and wealthy.
You said earlier that people want to elect someone who they perceive as sincere. But take someone like Susan Collins, who has been an enormously successful Republican politician in a blue state. I have no idea what Susan Collins actually thinks about abortion, but my gut feeling would be that, if Susan Collins actually thought that abortion was evil and Roe v. Wade should be overturned, her constituents in a blue state would not enjoy hearing that from her. Moreover, when I hear El-Sayed’s answers about defunding the police, I get confused, because it does seem to me that sometimes the wing of the Party that wants to focus the most on economic issues is in fact the most averse to changing its position on social issues.
Well, I do think our candidates come from places of conviction and sincerity, and have wrestled with their own personal views, and often are comfortable telling you that they are not poll-testing them. Often, this is why the tweets come back to hurt them, because they are really sharing with you, in a first-person sense, some core convictions. And what I think you’re correctly observing is that, O.K., well, you get into a political arena, and now your job is not to represent merely yourself but to represent others.
I do think you’re right that sometimes, on the progressive left, there’s a sense that too often a candidate who has come to a deep core conviction cannot be moved off of it. And I don’t think it does a service to politics itself if you operate that way. Politics is about persuasion. But I think part of the honest conversation about why progressives are doing well—and can and will win elections this cycle—is that I think there’s a hunger on the American public’s part, particularly born of Trump, that sees and watches him, and says, Here’s a guy who continues to yell that the election is rigged, and I think a lot of people just say, That’s probably a feeling he has, right? But we’re going to forgive him, you know, to some degree, right? Like, this is why he wins all these battleground states.
Do we think he won because he said that the election was rigged or in spite of it?
I’m saying he won in spite of it. I’m saying that working-class people say, You’re totally off and wrong on that one. However, there are other issues and other important things that matter to me, and if you can tell me that you’re persuadable around some of these other things, maybe I’ll give allowance for things that I might also disagree with you on.
If you look across the swing states with elections this fall, you have a lot of popular Democratic governors and senators: Jon Ossoff, Josh Shapiro, Gretchen Whitmer, Tony Evers. I would not call any of them left-wing. I would say some of them seem pretty poll-tested in the way they communicate. And they’re all pretty popular. How do you understand that?
We’re merging two conversations. One is politics, one’s policy. So we could have a conversation about the ways in which some of those people you just mentioned would fare in the politicking for President. I suspect it might be a little bit different for them, despite their popularity in the states they represent. Take Steve Bullock, the popular former governor of Montana: How does he fare if he runs for President?
Well, there’s a question of how he would run in a general election versus how he would run in a primary.
Right, exactly. But I’m saying that there is a different question, politics versus policy. Right now, when I look at some of those governors, there’s a feeling, in my view, that some people have no sense of choosing who their governor is. It’s the governor, and they are rewarding and appreciating the governor for just doing the job. There’s an element of competency. You are signed up to do a job, make sure you care about it. You know, the trash is picked up, the roads are fixed and repaired, the benefits are going out on due schedule.
But there’s no contest, no primary, and they are not having to face an alternative. I might not always agree with everything Josh Shapiro says, but, if you put me in Pennsylvania, I agree. Hey, thank you, Governor. You’re doing a fine job.
He’s gonna win reëlection pretty handily, it seems like.
Probably, yeah. But also, if you had a progressive governor who was doing the job, I suspect they would also be popular. You know, there is a progressive mayor of New York City who is doing a fine job. If you do the job, once you get into office, it’s critical that now you are there to show competence and professionalism.
I want to go back to 2024. There was a Democratic President helping fund the war in Gaza, and there was real anger about the role that the Biden Administration was playing in perpetuating massive war crimes and other horrible, horrible things in the conflict. And there was real anger at the establishment for it. Now, in 2026, there is still anger at the establishment over Gaza, but it seems like there is rage at the Democratic establishment across the board, on every issue. How did that happen?
I think that Gaza and the Middle East policy always represented something much larger than the humanitarian catastrophe that we all witnessed there. One of those things was a sense from so many Democrats that we were all seeing this injustice, and we knew it was an injustice, and Democratic politicians were unwilling to show accountability over it. And, therefore, they were deemed to be weak, and soft, and not strong leaders. So the qualities associated with Democrats to this day, right, if we were to think about the adjectives being used by your average Democratic activist, they’ll say the Democratic Party is weak.

Those were issues to do with mental acuity, and very little about the policy debate.
You aren’t saying you think Biden should have stayed in the race, right?
At that point, Senator Sanders was saying, If we change horses, the agenda may not be as strong for working-class people, and we may lose to Donald Trump.
I don’t assume you want to say that Biden should have stayed in the race, though, right?
I don’t want to speak for Senator Sanders, right? So I want his—you know, it’s a tough place for me to be in, because I, you know, I—on the one hand, I am, you know, I am a supporter of Bernie Sanders. In my mind, there’s a high level of consistency in Senator Sanders advocating, as the Senate Budget Committee chairman, for the Biden Administration’s American Rescue Plan, talking it up at every turn, and saying this was very meaningful to working-class people. He was being honest and clear with people that he was pushing the President of the United States to do these things, and he was prepared to tell people that these are positive developments for working-class people. He kept his word on that.
I went back to the op-ed that Bernie wrote about why Biden should stay in the race. And I noticed that he critiqued the “corporate” media for obsessively focussing on the debate. And then when Graham Platner was denying the rape accusation against him, Platner said it was the “corporate” media going after him. El-Sayed’s spokesperson blamed the “corporate” establishment when Governor Gretchen Whitmer endorsed his opponent. Do you find this cynical, or potentially playing into the hands of the far right, which feeds on distrust of institutions?
So, along with Senator Sanders, I run a working-class-journalism organization, and, from my vantage point, we are telling stories of corporate greed and corporate influence that have millions and millions of views, and people are interested in watching and consuming this content. And yet I think a lot of our critique has long been that much of the media doesn’t find these stories sexy.
I’m not arguing with that. But when Graham Platner is accused of rape and says that the corporate media is out to get him, I think we know what he’s trying to imply here. And I worry that there is a cynicism to that, which is pretty toxic. You’re accused of misbehavior with women, and you say the corporate media is out to get you. What kind of message do you think that sends to voters?
That’s not a great message. We can agree.
I want a media that feels a responsibility to say that the issues of economic justice are meaningful and important to me because they’re meaningful and important to a lot of other people. You’re right to say, If somebody accuses somebody of sexual assault or rape, that is a meaningful and important story. There’s no downplaying it. It is fundamental to a political race and to the integrity of a human being. So, yes, it’s important. And I think there’s a lot of frustration from progressive people that says, Well, when I go and talk about the issues of labor, the issues of antitrust, the issues of corporate taxation, those you find less interesting, and that therefore builds in a cynicism on behalf of some of these candidates, some of it earned, by the media. It’s not to discount or say that the issues you raised are fundamentally important. Don’t hear me say that. ♦

news.title: Democrats’ surging left wing faces a test in Michigan: Older Black voters
news.text:
She came to see Rep. James Clyburn, a civil rights icon for her generation, and he didn’t disappoint. “It brought tears to my eyes,” says Aarolyn McCullough, as she left the union hall in Detroit after hearing the Democrat from South Carolina speak.

The retired postal worker had already cast her ballot for Rep. Haley Stevens, the candidate Mr. Clyburn is backing in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary. “She gets things done,” Ms. McCullough says.

Black voters like Ms. McCullough are poised to play a decisive role in the marquee Aug. 4 race between Ms. Stevens, a centrist U.S. House member from suburban Detroit, and Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive former public health official. The expensive and acrimonious Senate contest has become a proxy battle for the Democratic Party’s future, spotlighting internal racial and generational divisions over everything from healthcare to immigration to aid for Israel. As the party grapples with a surge of energy on its left flank that’s toppled some longtime incumbents, Black Democrats, who have historically tended to back more moderate candidates, could hand the progressive movement a high-profile defeat – or its biggest victory yet.

Polls show Ms. Stevens, who is white, has an edge among Black voters overall, particularly older ones, while Dr. El-Sayed leads among younger and college-educated voters of all races. At the same time, the Black vote – long a cornerstone of the Democratic base – is itself increasingly divided along age and education lines.

A flood of Michigan heavy-hitters, including Gov. Gretchen Whitmer and retiring Sen. Gary Peters, have lined up behind Ms. Stevens, along with members of the national establishment, such as Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York. Dr. El-Sayed, meanwhile, has the backing of progressive figures such as Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont, Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York.

How it all plays out – and how Tuesday’s winner fares against former congressman Mike Rogers, the expected GOP nominee, in the fall – could reframe the debate over the direction of the party, including what type of candidate Democrats should nominate for president in 2028. In 2020, Black voters in South Carolina played a key role in stopping a surging Mr. Sanders and delivering the Democratic presidential nomination to Joe Biden. For the 2028 cycle, the Democratic National Committee voted in July to change the primary calendar so South Carolina will cast the very first votes.

Both campaigns are working to turn out the vote in Detroit, a majority Black city that has more than 500,000 registered voters. Only 1 in 5, however, usually vote in party primaries.

Kendyll Lavat, a healthcare worker, brought her ballot to a “get out the vote” block party in downtown Detroit on Saturday. She says she is leaning toward Ms. Stevens, despite misgivings about the lawmaker’s support for data centers, because she sees her as the better bet to win in the fall. “It’s important to me that the candidate has the potential to win in November,” she says.

Ms. Lavat, who is Black, praises Dr. El-Sayed’s support for universal healthcare, but is hesitant to vote for him. The candidate has been hit by a slew of negative ads; one spot accuses him of “disrespecting women,” which his campaign calls misleading and offensive. “I don’t see much positive support for him, so I’m concerned that he will have a lot of roadblocks,” Ms. Lavat says.

A generational schism

Dr. El-Sayed’s far-left platform – which calls for Medicare-for-all, abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and ending all U.S. aid to Israel – echoes those of democratic socialist candidates who have recently surged to victory in primaries in blue states (though Dr. El-Sayed does not call himself a democratic socialist). Those ideas might face more of an uphill climb in a swing state such as Michigan.

Speaking to reporters in Flint, Dr. El-Sayed refuted criticism that his campaign hasn’t connected with Black voters, pointing to his years of community work as a public health official. “I try to make a habit of showing up and delivering, and that’s the basis of the support that we’re earning in and around Detroit, Wayne County, and in the Black community,” he says.

Younger voters are more likely to support progressive candidates than their elders, who remember the Jim Crow era and have a strong sense of loyalty to the Democratic establishment. Older Black voters also tend to hold more conservative views on LGBTQ+ issues, as well as issues such as immigration and policing, that put them out of step with progressives.

Keith Williams, a Stevens supporter who chairs the Michigan Democratic Party Black Caucus, says Black voters often take the long view, recognizing that lasting change comes slowly. “You don’t have enough votes in this country to do an all-out universal healthcare,” he says. “It’s a process. You can’t get it all in one go.”

In New York City’s 2025 mayoral primary, Zohran Mamdani faced similar questions to Dr. El-Sayed about his levels of Black support. In that race, Mr. Clyburn endorsed former New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo, who was Black voters’ first choice overall in the ranked-choice contest. But while Mr. Cuomo won 60-and-over voters by 28 percentage points, the reverse was true among Black voters under 50, where Mr. Mamdani had a 42-point advantage.

Cheryl Hermann, a Black nurse in Detroit who is volunteering for Dr. El-Sayed’s campaign, says the generational divide is real – as is the frustration at current Democratic leadership. Younger voters think “we’ve sold them out to corporate interests” and want to see systemic change, she says.

Chatting before a rally for Dr. El-Sayed in a Detroit suburb, Ms. Hermann downplays the significance of the mostly white crowd, saying it’s not reflective of the campaign’s outreach. While Black voters might not be heavily represented at this particular event, she says, “Don’t think they’re not going to vote [for Dr. El-Sayed]. Because they will.”

From the auto industry to Israel

Ms. Stevens has been focused on pocketbook issues, vowing to resist President Donald Trump’s tariffs that she says are hurting manufacturing and pushing up consumer prices. “When Michigan is in a moment of crisis, I’m running at it. And I’m winning for us,” she said in her speech at the Detroit union hall.

She also emphasizes her past role in the 2009 federal auto bailout under “the legendary, incredible 44th President” – a line that is roundly applauded here in Detroit, where Barack Obama’s presidency was a high-water mark for many Black voters. Ms. Stevens served as chief of staff in Mr. Obama’s auto bailout task force, which is credited with saving between 150,000 and 200,000 jobs in Michigan. The largest union in Michigan, the United Auto Workers, has endorsed Dr. El-Sayed.

But Ms. Stevens’ most potent argument to primary voters might be around the question of electability. Democrats are in an uphill battle to retake control of the Senate, and they cannot afford to lose any Democratic-held seats, including Michigan.

“I’m going to be real. Mike Rogers said it the other day. He wants Abdul to win. We’re not going to let that happen,” Ms. Stevens said, speaking of the likely Republican nominee.

Last week, CNN reported that Mr. Rogers had told supporters on a private call that he was confident of beating Dr. El-Sayed because he was “so radical.”

Ms. Stevens has benefited from as much as $30 million in spending by the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, which has become a lightning rod for progressives who oppose military aid to Israel.

Dr. El-Sayed has refused to accept outside money and vows, if elected, to curb such election spending. “Ask yourself why they would spend that much money to beat me if I wasn’t absolutely serious about opposing their power in our government,” Dr. El-Sayed tells a group of supporters gathered in a fluorescent-lit office in a Flint strip mall.

Michigan has the country’s highest percentage of Arab Americans relative to its population, some of whom turned against the Biden administration over Israel’s war in Gaza, helping Mr. Trump flip the battleground state in 2024.

In the Detroit area, there is still lingering resentment toward Muslim voters who joined the “Uncommitted” movement opposing Mr. Biden during the Democratic primary. Dr. El-Sayed was part of that movement, but then endorsed Kamala Harris as the nominee. Other Democrats in majority-Arab cities either stayed home or voted for Mr. Trump over Ms. Harris.

Some Democrats privately worry about the barriers that a Muslim American candidate could face in a statewide race.

But Kandia Milton, an ally of Dr. El-Sayed who chairs The Black Slate, a political organization, says no one thought Mr. Mamdani had a shot in New York either. “We keep writing candidates off because of their race or because they’re too ‘progressive.’ There is a movement of people looking for candidates who are not wedded to the established ways of politics,” he says.
news.summary: Tuesday’s primary for Michigan’s open Senate seat is serving as a proxy battle over the Democratic Party’s future. How it all plays out could shape the 2028 presidential race.
news.author: Simon Montlake

news.title: Republicans Handed Worrisome Signs in New North Carolina Senate Poll
news.text: A new North Carolina Senate poll from Fox News has delivered fresh warning signs for Republicans, showing former Democratic Governor Roy Cooper with a healthy advantage over Republican Michael Whatley in one of the nation's most closely watched races for the upper chamber. Cooper leads the former Republican National Committee chairman by 9 percentage points overall with 53 percent compared to 44 percent, underscoring Democrats' growing confidence that they could flip a seat that will be critical in the battle for control of the Senate. The survey's likely more concerning numbers for Republicans, however, extend beyond the overall margin. Democrats appear far more energized ahead of the midterm elections, with 51 percent of Democratic voters saying they are "extremely interested" in the election compared with just 42 percent of Republicans. Democratic enthusiasm is also evident in voter motivation, as 58 percent of Democrats say they are extremely motivated to cast a ballot versus 50 percent of Republicans. Those figures suggest Democrats currently hold the intensity advantage that could prove decisive in midterm elections. Newsweek reached out to Cooper and Whatley's campaigns via email Wednesday night for comment. What To Know That enthusiasm gap is translating directly into Cooper's electoral strength. Among voters who say they are extremely interested in the election, Cooper's lead expands dramatically to 57 percent versus 42 percent for Whatley—a commanding 15-point advantage, the poll shows. The Democrat also posts a 13-point lead, 55 percent to 42 percent, among voters who describe themselves as extremely motivated to vote. Among those who say they are "certain" to vote, Cooper maintains his 9-point advantage, 53 percent to 44 percent. Those are particularly troubling numbers for Republicans because highly engaged voters are the most likely to turn out on Election Day, making enthusiasm a key factor for potential electoral performance. "Recent data put the average Republican advantage in North Carolina statewide races at about 3 points," Republican pollster Daron Shaw, who conducts the survey alongside Democrat Chris Anderson, said in the Fox News poll. "Cooper’s edge rests on almost unanimous Democratic support and commanding numbers among independents. To win, Whatley must stop the bleeding with non-MAGA Republicans and improve his standing with disaffected, less partisan Carolinians." Among independents, Cooper holds a 60 to 34 percent advantage over Whatley, the poll shows. Whatley's favorability in the poll is 40 percent compared to a 46 percent unfavorable rating, while Cooper's favorability is 54 percent compared to an unfavorable rating of 44 percent. Why Is the North Carolina Race So Important? The Tar Heel State's contest is critical because it's expected to help determine control of the U.S. Senate. Republicans hold a 53-45 majority—excluding independent Senators Bernie Sanders and Angus King, who caucus with Democrats—and Democrats view flipping the North Carolina seat as among their few viable paths to reclaiming the upper chamber, while Republicans see it as essential to maintaining their lead. The race will likely be among the most competitive races in this year's midterms, after Republican Thom Tillis opted against running for another term. But federal races in North Carolina have proved elusive for Democrats, who have not won the state at the Senate or presidential level since 2008. Trump narrowly won the state in the 2024 presidential election over then-Vice President Kamala Harris, by over 3 points. The findings also add to a growing body of polling that has consistently shown Cooper with the upper hand in the race. Recent surveys have pointed to the former governor's strong statewide popularity, while election forecasters have shifted the contest toward Democrats. With North Carolina expected to be one of the marquee Senate battlegrounds of the 2026 midterms, Republicans will likely need to close the enthusiasm gap and consolidate their base if Whatley hopes to erase Cooper's advantage in the few months ahead. What Other Polling Shows A Public Policy Polling survey this month shows Cooper up 48 percent compared to Whatley's 44 percent. The poll surveyed 759 North Carolina voters on July 10 and July 11 and had a margin of error of 3.6 percent. In a New York Times/Siena University poll, Cooper held a 7-point lead over Whatley with 50 percent compared to 43 percent. The poll surveyed 601 likely voters from June 15 to June 27 and had a margin of error of 4.7 percent. The Cook Political Report has ranked the race in the "lean Democrat" category.
news.summary: The Tar Heel State's contest is critical, as it will likely help determine control of the U.S. Senate.

news.title: Fast Takes: Leave the theatrics to Hollywood, Dems outgrew common sense and more
news.text:
Democrat: Leave the Theatrics to Hollywood

The US entertainment industry’s “gloriously cutthroat” spirit “makes America the cultural center of the world and a domestic economic growth engine,” but the suit by a dozen blue-state attorneys general to “block the acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery by Paramount Skydance puts it all at risk” with bogus antitrust claims, warns Ari Emanuel at The Wall Street Journal. In their “trash” antitrust case, the AGs “pretend Amazon MGM, A24 and Lionsgate don’t exist” though their films have grossed billions already this year. The merged firm’s “27% share of feature-film box office” won’t “substantially lessen competition”; indeed, the deal leaves the new company “committed to at least 30 theatrical releases a year.” “The harm doesn’t begin when the attorneys general win their suit,” it began when money started to pour “into legal fees rather than productions.” “Let Hollywood creatives get back to trying to rip each other’s heads off . . . it’s what we’re best at.”

Conservative: Dems Outgrew Common Sense

Elon Musk in a recent interview offered “a powerful diagnosis of the growing gulf between America and Europe, Republicans and Democrats, ‘normal people’ and the mainstream media,” remarks USA Today’s Nicole Russell. The interviewer claimed Musk “supports not just the populist right but the far right — in fact, very fringe parties”; he replied, “No, I support the normal people. What you call the far right, falsely.” Russell continues: He dared his questioner “to consider that 10 to 15 years ago, Obama and Clinton held the same views on immigration and other issues that Trump holds today, views the ‘lunatic left’ now brands far right.” At every level of government, “commonsense ideas Democrats once agreed on are now dismissed as fringe” and: “The chasm between right and left” is “dug deeper by the media.”

Libertarian: Too Many Elex Over From the Start

Some 150 House races this year “had no meaningful competition,” gripes Reason’s Eric Boehm, with incumbents “all but guaranteed another two years in office after running unopposed in their primaries” in districts that are super-safe red or blue seats — leaving more than 84 million Americans “effectively disenfranchised.” California, Washington and Hawaii now have “open, all-candidate primaries,” leaving only five of their 63 House seats uncontested. Yes, that often means “two candidates from the same party advancing” to the general, but it beats watching more than one-third of candidates win before the election even starts. “Americans should be embracing any and all ideas that aim to make elections more competitive.”

Historian: DSA Takeover Was By Invitation

The socialist “takeover of the Democratic Party” wasn’t sparked by concerns about ‘affordability,’ ” but “was merely the logical culmination of . . . radicalism within the Democratic aristocracy,” including “Elizabeth Warren, Kamala Harris, and Hakeem Jeffries,” contends Victor Davis Hanson at American Greatness. “Mainstream Democrats” spread nearly every “weaponized scam and national hysteria in the last two decades.” Did the “Democratic apparat calm the waters,” when “three would-be assassins got close enough to killing Trump?” Did they “at least pretend to deplore the violence” against ICE? No, socialists “did not hijack the party;” they “were spawned and nurtured by aged Democrats,” adding only antisemitism. “America will soon see how this insanity works out.”

Urbanist: Rent Freeze at Real Risk

In response to the Rent Guidelines Board vote “to fulfill the mayor’s campaign promise” of a “rent freeze,” a group of “affected property owners” have sued “to nullify” that 0% hike, notes City Journal’s John Ketcham. A politically-motivated vote “could constitute a violation of due process.” The law requires the RGB to “weigh evidence of certain economic factors” in its deliberations, yet the “evidence before the RGB — based upon the board’s own research — does not support” the freeze, since it found landlords’ expenses up 5.3% in the last year. Plus, multiple board members have well-documented “histories of anti-owner bias,” also supporting “a finding that the RGB’s decision was arbitrary and capricious.”

— Compiled by The Post Editorial Board
news.summary: The Wall Street Journal's Ari Emanuel slams the lawsuit blocking the Warner Bros.-Paramount merger, while NYC landlords sue to nullify a rent freeze.

news.title: Trump rejected $227m in disaster relief to blue states after FEMA OK’d the money
news.text:
President Trump reportedly rejected $227 million in disaster aid requests this month from four Democrat-led states, despite federal disaster officials certifying that damage in these areas hit established thresholds to trigger federal aid.

In the wake of a record-setting snowstorm that hit the East Coast in February, New Jersey, New York, Massachusetts and Rhode Island sought federal assistance.

Regional offices of the Federal Emergency Management Agency and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration affirmed the extent of the need in New Jersey, Massachusetts and Rhode Island, according to documents obtained by Politico, while officials in New York told the outlet they also had a request rejected despite administration officials allegedly concluding it met federal standards.

In one alleged example, FEMA's New England office certified more than $19 million of damages in Rhode Island, more than nine times FEMA's usual cost threshold for the state.

President Trump still rejected the request despite this analysis, a highly unusual move, according to disaster experts.

"I can't think of a time a declaration was denied," a former FEMA official told Politico.

The Independent has contacted the White House and NOAA for comment.

"FEMA assesses a number of factors to determine the severity, magnitude, and impact of a disaster event," the agency told The Independent. "Major disaster declaration request evaluation factors considered include estimated cost of the assistance, localized impacts, insurance coverage in force, hazard mitigation, recent multiple disasters, programs of other federal assistance, state fiscal capacity and resource availability, uninsured home and personal property losses, disaster-impacted population profile, impact to community infrastructure, casualties, and disaster related unemployment."

It declined to comment on whether the president had rejected any of its analyses about the snowstorm.

The Trump administration has denied political favoritism played into the July aid decision, which came two days after President Trump approved disaster aid to six Republican-led states. (In general, the president has approved nearly 90 percent of requests from states governed by members of his party, more than three times the rate of approvals for Democrat-led states, Politico previously found.)

Since the George W. Bush administration, presidents have approved all but one request for snow aid that meets FEMA standards, according to a recent analysis.

Last week, more than a dozen states sued the Trump administration, arguing it was wrongly trying to tie election and immigration policy demands to federal disaster aid.

The Trump administration has scoffed at the suit, calling it "partisan pushback" against "commonsense measures" from "leftwing politicians."

The Trump administration initially toyed with eliminating FEMA, though a Trump-backed review council recommended earlier this year that the agency instead share more work with state and local governments while streamlining its processes.

Lawmakers are considering a bipartisan bill to elevate FEMA from its place inside the Department of Homeland Security to an independent, Cabinet-level agency, while expediting payments to survivors.

The Trump administration has often sought to use federal funding as a cudgel to force Democratic and liberal jurisdictions into policy changes, especially in higher education, where the White House has threatened to cut off billions of dollars in support to targeted university systems.

In court documents this month, the administration admitted that it canceled a block of roughly $7.5 billion in Biden-era clean energy funding "based solely" on the fact the money was flowing to projects in Democratic-led states.

The cuts were not based on "any programmatic, statutory, cost-reduction, or performance-based factor," the Department of Energy conceded as part of early negotiations in a federal lawsuit from University of California researchers.

Instead, the grants were included on a list of cancellations announced in October "based solely on the political identity of the grant recipient's state, i.e., whether the recipient's location and/or place of performance was in a Blue State or a non-Blue State."

The department added that with one exception, 284 terminated grants were slated to fund projects in Democratic-led states or states that voted for Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris in 2024. The roughly 340 grants that survived the chopping block were "in a state that awarded its electoral votes to President Trump in the 2024 election" or had at least one Republican senator, according to court filings.
news.author: Josh Marcus

news.title: America is clear: It doesn’t like older lawmakers (but keeps voting for them anyway)
news.text:
Most Americans think lawmakers in Congress are just too old, according to a new poll, as Washington reels from the death of Sen. Lindsey Graham, 71, and the lengthy hospitalization of Sen. Mitch McConnell, 84.

About 58 percent of Americans think the share of elderly lawmakers in Congress, which is currently one of the oldest in U.S. history, is a major problem, per a new CNN / SSRS poll.

That share rises to 68 percent for respondents younger than age 35.

Two-thirds of Americans, meanwhile, told the poll that elected officials should release all medical information about conditions that might impact their ability to serve. Just 25 percent thought politicians have the same right as regular citizens to keep their health records private.

And a whopping 70 percent of people aligned with the major parties said they would be uneasy or upset if the Republicans or Democrats nominated someone over age 70 for office.

The average age of Congress has been creeping up for decades, and the median age of current U.S. senators is 66, a disproportionately high age compared with the general population. 

Age concerns are back in the spotlight thanks to years of recent political turmoil.

In 2023, Sen. Dianne Feinstein died in office at age 90 while facing calls to step down amid questions about her declining memory and numerous health complications.

The following year, concerns about President Joe Biden’s health and mental fitness tanked his reelection campaign and led to Kamala Harris replacing him on the ballot. 

The trend has cut across parties and administrations.

President Trump has faced persistent questions about his own health and fitness, given that he regularly appears to fall asleep at public events and often is seen with bandages and makeup for a persistent medical condition on his hand.

In the Senate, Mitch McConnell of Kentucky has been absent from congressional business for more than 40 days after a fall in his home in June left him unconscious.

The senator has insisted he’s on the road to recovery, and has shared multiple photos and written statements updating the public about his condition.

Critics have argued the senator needs to do more to assure the public he can still serve.

Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, a Democrat, has demanded in a letter to the senator on Monday that he “directly and verbally address the people of Kentucky and provide proof of your capacity to serve, or resign.” 

“If you are unwilling to voluntarily show that you still have the capacity to serve, I will insist Leader Thune fully investigate your condition, report to the American people, and begin the process if warranted,” Beshear added.

The Kentucky governor has also challenged CNN to call McConnell live on air, given claims from CNN contributor Scott Jennings that he recently spoke on the phone with McConnell. 

Age concerns have inspired calls for term limits and a more transparent process for evaluating and disclosing the health of lawmakers and candidates.

“The U.S. political system has virtually no objective standards to ensure that the people entrusted with the highest offices in the country remain physically and cognitively capable of performing some of the most important and demanding jobs in the world,” Anahita Dua, a vascular surgeon, wrote in a recent MS Now opinion piece. “That is no longer acceptable.”
news.summary: The recent death of Sen. Lindsey Graham and hospitalization of Sen. Mitch McConnell has reignited debate over whether lawmakers are too old to serve
news.author: Josh Marcus

news.title: Jim Clyburn is pointing the finger at all the wrong people
news.text:
In a recent podcast interview, Rep. Jim Clyburn, D-S.C., blamed Black voters in part for Vice President Kamala Harris’ loss in the 2024 presidential election. Clyburn typified a retrograde assumption many in the Democratic establishment hold: that certain voters ought to serve the party rather than the other way around. With the midterm elections looming and the start of a high-stakes presidential primary season around the corner, hearing such a dismissive view of voters expressed by a Democrat of Clyburn’s influence is particularly alarming.

Clyburn made that comment during a conversation with Vox’s Astead Herndon, who pressed the 86-year-old, 17-term representative to assign blame for the Democratic Party’s low approval ratings, including with its own voters. Clyburn, a former chair of the Congressional Black Caucus and a former House majority whip, blamed everyone but party leadership. The conversation got especially pointed when he and Herndon discussed Harris’ 2024 loss and Herndon asked Clyburn if he thought there was a political lesson to take from an administration whose central goal was to stop Donald Trump’s return to the White House. Clyburn answered: “When the white vote turned out 71% two years ago, and the Black vote turned out 59%, you tell me whose fault that is.” He later added that if that “59% had been 69%, she would have won.” When Herndon followed by asking if Clyburn was saying “Black people let Kamala Harris down,” he responded, “In many instances, absolutely.” 

Clyburn’s answer was an astonishing deflection.

Parties are not owed votes; they earn them. And racial minorities and marginalized communities — whether they are Black, women or Latino — shouldn’t be taken for granted as a lock for the Democratic Party just because it’s the party that embraces multiculturalism.

Politicians are supposed to be public servants.

Clyburn’s statement is sadly emblematic of establishment Democrats’ tendency to see ethnic minority voters only as people who vote as monolithic blocs. But they don’t. Just like white voters, they have interests across many policy areas — the economy, immigration, taxes, foreign policy and so on. And just like white voters, they can change their mind, be ambivalent about candidates and think in terms of strategic trade-offs. In the 2024 election, voters across all kinds of demographics were dissatisfied with the economy in the wake of a surge in inflation. The Democratic Party didn’t take their concerns seriously enough, and a candidate deploying Hitlerian rhetoric made gains with Latinos, Black men and Asian Americans compared with his first victory. 

There is some historical context that distinguishes Clyburn’s perspective from those of other members of party leadership. He grew up in the segregated South, where the battle for voting rights was won and where, after the Voting Rights Act became law, many Black people saw voting as a sacred duty. Black political power was and is deeply intertwined with participation in Democratic politics. But taking that vote for granted is antidemocratic, and can even be exploitative — and it does not obviate the need to listen to a community’s needs and perceptions. “Is there no reason that Black voters could not have felt heard” by the Democrats, Herndon asked Clyburn. “There might be. I’d like to know what it is,” Clyburn responded, seemingly implying that he couldn’t conceive of a good one or that no such reasonable views are out there.

Politicians are supposed to be public servants, and parties succeed in politics when they recognize the old adage about effective customer service: The customer is always right. (Or least needs to be understood and attended to in some fashion.) Sensitivity to what voters want in real time — rather than banking on the lesser-evil ballot or some fixed notion of what’s best for voters even when they say otherwise — is what helps parties build trust, identify sources of excitement and drive up voter turnout. That’s how you push that number up from 59%.

Clyburn’s blinkered worldview is consequential. He has been in Congress for more than three decades and served as House majority whip multiple times. His capacity as a power broker helped Joe Biden win the Democratic presidential nomination in 2020. Yet in that Vox interview, he strongly rejected the idea that Democratic leaders should engage in any big-picture introspection about what the party stands for. At various points, he blamed “media branding” for its beleaguered reputation. He said progressive challengers knocking out Democratic incumbents in the primaries does not signal a problem with the party but was the fault of individual low-performing candidates. Herndon interviewed Clyburn on his 86th birthday, and not surprisingly, Clyburn rejected the idea that the advanced age of many in the party is cause for concern. 

In what may be the most tragicomic example of being out of touch, Clyburn admitted that he hadn’t heard of ChatGPT until the week before the interview. No concern there. ChatGPT only symbolizes the way huge swaths of the workforce may eventually face job market apocalypse. Why should a politician of such influence know anything about the buzziest economic issue of recent years? 

Remarkably, Clyburn’s influence within the Democratic Party is still growing — with South Carolina jumping to the start of the Democratic presidential primary schedule, his role as kingmaker is larger than ever. But like so many Democrats of his generation, his ability to understand and influence the world itself is waning.
